title: The Guardian SecureDrop
text:
SecureDrop is a tool to help people securely send messages and documents to the Guardian. It uses the Tor network to preserve source anonymity by hiding where messages came from. All communication is encrypted in transit and on our server. To avoid surveillance and interception, submissions from sources are decrypted on a device that is isolated from both the internet and our internal networks.
To access our SecureDrop site you need to use a browser application that can access the Tor network.
Use of the Tor network helps hide your identity online, but it does not guarantee the safety of the computer that you use to contact us. We recommend that you avoid accessing SecureDrop from small networks where use of a Tor browser may be monitored or restricted. If there is any risk of your browser activity being recorded, it's advisable not to jump straight from this information page to the actual Guardian SecureDrop site. You could instead make a note of the SecureDrop ‘onion’ URL (see below) and then wait to connect to that site at another time or on a different computer.
If SecureDrop is not the right tool for you, please consider some of the other options in our interactive guide: How to contact the Guardian securely.

title: How to contact the Guardian
author: Guardian Staff; Guardian staff reporter
text:
Customer Services
For any queries including subscription related queries, please visit our Help centre, where you will also find contact details for your region.
Head Offices
You can find Customer Service contact details on our Help Centre.
UK main office
Please address written correspondence to: The Guardian, Kings Place, 90 York Way, London, N1 9GU, United Kingdom.
 The switchboard number for the London office of the Guardian and the Guardian website is: 020 3353 2000 (or if dialling from overseas: +44 20 3353 2000). Please do not use this number for Customer Service queries as our switchboard team will not be able to answer your query or direct you to Customer Service.
US main office
Contact details for the Guardian US office
Australia main office
Contact details for the Guardian Australia office
How to contact editorial departments and desks
Please take care to send queries to the correct destination as there is no guarantee that messages will be forwarded.
To send us story tips confidentially
For information on how to contact Guardian journalists securely please read this guide. We recommend you use the Secure Messaging tool in the Guardian app, or our SecureDrop portal.
To contact a member of staff
 Individual staff, whether editorial or commercial, can be contacted using this email format:
- 
  Firstname.lastname@theguardian.com 
Letters to the editor
  Letters for publication in the Guardian should be sent to the addresses below. The sender’s full postal address and phone number are required, for verification only. For further guidance on submitting a letter, click here.
  Guardian: guardian.letters@theguardian.com
Corrections and clarifications of editorial content – the readers’ editor
 It is the policy of the Guardian to correct significant editorial errors and handle editorial complaints as soon as possible. The readers’ editors are independent internal ombudsmen and can be contacted as follows:
Elisabeth Ribbans – Guardian global readers’ editor
  guardian.readers@theguardian.com
Guardian readers’ editor page
Please note that queries about subscriptions, vouchers, reader offers, advertising, marketing and other non-editorial areas are not handled by the readers’ editors. These should be addressed to the relevant non-editorial departments. Story suggestions should also be sent to the relevant editorial departments.
Legal complaints
 Legal complaints should be addressed to our Editorial Legal Services department at: Kings Place, 90 York Way, London, N1 9GU
Moderation
  For more information about moderation and to contact the moderation team, please see this page.
The Guardian: editorial departments and desks
- 
  Arts desk: culture@theguardian.com or arts@theguardian.com 
- 
  Consumer investigative column in weekly Money section consumer.champions@theguardian.com 
- 
  Environment desk: environment.desk@theguardian.com 
- 
  Film desk: culture@theguardian.com 
- 
  The Filter: thefilter@theguardian.com 
- 
  Music: culture@theguardian.com 
- 
  Notes and queries: nq@theguardian.com 
- 
  Obituaries desk: obituaries@theguardian.com 
- 
  Opinion desk: opinion@theguardian.com 
- 
  Pictures: for emails from readers, agencies and PRs picturedesk@theguardian.com 
- 
  Pictures: for advisories on film openings, PR openings and similar: photocalls@theguardian.com 
- 
  Portfolios/artwork: for emails from illustrators, animators and their agents: illustration.portfolios@theguardian.com 
- 
  Travel desk: travel@theguardian.com 
Freelance contributions
If you would like to contribute freelance content, please ensure you have read our Contributors’ guide.
Story pitches should be sent to the relevant editorial department, as listed above.
Any queries you have relating to the freelance charter, or other terms and conditions for the supply of content to GNM, should be directed to our Rights department at rights@theguardian.com
Guardian Foundation
The Guardian Foundation is a charity whose purpose is to promote global press freedom and access to liberal journalism. They work directly with journalists, news organisations, audiences and educators, in schools and across communities to enable change.
Contact The Guardian Foundation here.
Report a suspected security vulnerability
If you spot a potential security vulnerability in the Guardian’s websites and apps, or suspicious Guardian emails/articles/endorsements, we’d be grateful to hear from you. Please send an email to icrt@theguardian.com with the subject line “Suspected security vulnerability”. If possible, include screenshots in your description. We may contact you for more details. Thanks for your help.
Please note we do not operate a bug bounty or responsible disclosure program at present.
Back issues and circulation
For information on ordering a back issue of the Guardian, click here.
If your query concerns UK distribution or retail supplies please contact business.information@theguardian.com. Otherwise all Customer Service queries must go through Customer Service, visit our Help centre for contact details for your region.
Advertisers, sponsorship and e-commerce
To find out more about all advertising and sponsorship opportunities in the Guardian and the Guardian website, click here.
If you have a question or concern about an advert on the site please report the problem here.
Press office
If you are a journalist with a media inquiry, please visit the press office page for the relevant contact information.
Employment and work experience
If you are interested in working for Guardian News and Media, please see our dedicated careers site at theguardian.com/workforus. All current work experience and internship schemes are detailed on this site under the “Other opportunities” heading.
Content distribution and syndication
For permission to re-publish Guardian content, or acquire a licence to re-distribute our content, please visit our Syndication website.
Film and TV adaptations
The Guardian’s award-winning journalism and 200+ year archive serve as the creative foundation for high-profile film, television, and theatre projects. Partnering with leading studios, producers, and streaming platforms, we bring unparalleled investigative depth and global stories from page to screen.
To discuss film and TV opportunities, please contact film.tv@theguardian.com

title: How to contact the Guardian securely
author: Luke Hoyland
text:
Confidential tips
 Journalists work closely with readers like you to investigate stories
					in the public interest. While no communication system is foolproof we
					go to great lengths to protect your identity. If you’re ready 
					to share information with a journalist, you’re in the right place, 
					and we will treat you as a confidential journalistic source.
 We rely on people sharing tips in the public interest – and we’re
					grateful that you’re thinking about getting in touch.
Composing your message
 We’re unlikely to pursue a lead unless we think it may lead to a news
					story, and we can't act on information that is vague or speculative.
					Our job is to hold power to account, to reveal institutional or
					systemic failings and to report on topics that are genuinely
					newsworthy. Please be clear, detailed and specific about your tip, why
					you think it matters, and what evidence you have.
Facts: Specifics are critical, such as names,
		locations and dates.
 I work at government department ‘Department name’ in 
		the procurement section.
 Clearly state the nature of your tip: Be concise 
		and focus on what you know, rather than what you think or suspect.
 I have discovered evidence of a senior official's 
		involvement in corruption and bribery. ‘Name’, the head of our 
		section, has received $150,000 in under-the-radar payments.
 Evidence: Tell us how you know what you know,
		and how we might verify it.
 I have photographic evidence of transactions 
		from the past two years and access to further 
		documents that show these were a quid pro quo for awarding 
		contracts to multinational company ‘Company name’.
 Choose your contact method
 There are many ways to contact the Guardian securely. Review the
				following options to see which one is best for you.
    SecureMessaging
 Share your story with a journalist.
			
			Securely & easily. Inside our news app.
 Pros:
 - Free and easy to download.
- End-to-end encrypted.
- Sending messages is indistinguishable from normal use of the Guardian app.
- Connects you, anonymously if you choose, directly to our journalists.
- Designed to be easy for everyone to use, without expert tech knowledge.
Consider other platforms:
 - If you live or work in a place where the Guardian app is not safe to
				have on your device, scroll down for alternative ways to contact us.
    Download the Guardian app
 1 of 3
Go to 'Secure Messaging' in the menu
 2 of 3
Follow the instructions onscreen
 3 of 3
 SecureDrop
 Our SecureDrop system is a great way to contact us and to send documents. However, it does require more technical preparation.
 Pros:
 - SecureDrop does not record where things come from.
- All material is encrypted automatically.
- We read your submissions on secure computers.
Cons:
 - You will need to download Tor software to access our SecureDrop system.
- If you are being watched, the very act of using Tor may arouse suspicion.
SecureDrop allows you to safely send us messages and documents, and to follow
	up with us later if you wish. All we get is what you send us plus a codename
	that allows us to reply to you. SecureDrop records nothing else about you. To
	prevent interception at our end, we decrypt any material that you send us on 
	a system that is completely offline.
 Get started:
 On a computer that you are confident is not being monitored, install Tor Browser. Then go to theguardian.com/securedrop and follow the instructions there.
 After that:
 When you first visit our SecureDrop site itself, you will be given a 
	passphrase before you can send anything. This phrase allows you to log back in 
	to view replies from us and to continue correspondence, if you so wish. 
	We do not always reply to messages and even when we do, responses can take several days.
 SecureDrop is quite a slow way to communicate, so after you have begun
	corresponding with a reporter they may suggest a more direct way to interact.
	You don’t have to agree to this, of course, but it can make things smoother
	under some circumstances.
 SecureDrop is an open source project managed by the Freedom of the Press Foundation.
      Instant messenger apps
 End to end encrypted messaging apps such as Signal and WhatsApp provide good protection for the content of your messages, and are very easy to use.
  Signal is trusted by journalists, human rights activists and security experts
	worldwide, and is our preferred instant messaging app. WhatsApp, while not 
	quite as secure, also encrypts the content of communications and benefits from 
	being so ubiquitous that using it is unlikely (in itself) to raise suspicion 
	in most parts of the world. Other secure messenger apps tend to be less widely 
	used for communication between sources and our journalists.
 Pros:
 - They’re very easy to use.
- They allow for speedy back-and-forth communication.
- Everything is encrypted in transit and on the service providers’ servers, so
		not even they can read the content of your messages.
Cons:
 - On WhatsApp, information about the participants in a conversation is less
		secure than the content itself.
- There are ways for very sophisticated adversaries, such as government spy 
		agencies, to ascertain that someone is communicating with a journalist 
		using messaging apps – even if they can’t read the message content.
- Instant messenger communication requires advance knowledge of the
		participants’ contact details. For WhatsApp it must be a phone number; for
		Signal it can be a username or phone number. Many journalists are reluctant
		to publish their personal contact details widely because such information 
		can be abused.
Conversations with journalists often shift from another method to instant 
	messenger apps once both sides have established some trust and have discussed 
	the benefits and risks. But you or the journalist may decide not to use them.
 Get started:
 Decide whether you want to do this on your normal phone or on a less easily 
	traceable phone. After installing the app, make it as secure as possible: 
	if there are extra authentication options, activate them. And activate 
	disappearing messages so your conversations don’t sit around forever 
	on your device.
 Read more about Signal here 
	and about WhatsApp here.
 After that:
 If you’re worried about surveillance and you’ve not used the app before,
	consider using it for few innocuous purposes first, such as exchanging 
	messages with friends. That way, when you message us, your use of the app 
	doesn’t look out of the ordinary.
 Check our journalists’ profile pages for contact details. Google their name 
	and ‘the Guardian’ and you should find them. If you can’t find the contact 
	details for the journalist you want to speak to, you could use another method
	such as Secure Messaging or SecureDrop to outline what you want to speak about
	and to provide your instant messenger contact details.
 Please note the recommendations earlier in this guide for what to say about 
	the information you wish to share.
      Email
 Use a tailor-made email account to make it less obvious that you are in contact with a journalist.
   If the information you wish to share with us isn’t extremely sensitive, 
	email is probably the easiest way to get in touch. Even so, you may 
	consider it worthwhile to put a bit of distance between your messages 
	to a journalist and the rest of your life. Plus, because journalists 
	receive so many emails, you should take extra care to make sure your 
	message doesn’t get lost in the noise.
 Pros:
 - Everyone knows how to use email, and many Guardian journalists publish
		their email addresses.
- You can send long messages and attachments. This is difficult using phone
		apps.
- It's possible (but not straightforward) to add encryption to email messages.
Cons:
 - Normal emails are not at all secure. Your correspondence can be monitored. 
		Even a purpose-built email account can reveal information about you.
- Adding encryption to emails is difficult and does not hide some information
		(who is talking to whom, the subject lines, etc).
Email is an inherently insecure medium but you can do some things to make your 
	correspondence less likely to be intercepted.
 Get started:
 Don’t use your regular work or personal email address. Create a new email account 
	solely for corresponding with the Guardian. Do this on a computer that can't easily
	be linked back to you.
 When you sign up for a new email account, make sure the sign-up information 
	you provide doesn’t tie the account back to you. Never use the same password 
	for different accounts.
 After that:
 Because it's so easy to send emails, journalists often receive a lot of spurious
	and irrelevant messages. So anything that doesn't get their attention quickly may 
	be overlooked. Read the advice further up in this guide about what makes a 
	good story tip.
 Information carried with an email message can reveal your IP address. 
	If you don’t want the location you send from to be traceable, connect to your 
	email service over the Tor network. or send from somewhere that doesn’t easily identify you.
 Remember to log out after sending the message. You may also wish to delete the 
	history of the correspondence from your browser or email software. Keep your computer secure.
 Some Guardian journalists publish PGP keys, allowing you to encrypt the content
	of email messages (but not the subject line or the fact that you are communicating with them).
	See theguardian.com/pgp.
 - You can email the Guardian's UK investigations team on 
		investigationsno.thanks.contact@thenot.here.eitherguardian.com.
   Telephone
 Although telephone communication is far from secure, it can be a practical way to get a conversation started.
    Pros:
 - Requires no technical prowess.
- Useful to initiate communication with a journalist to exchange contact
		information for more secure channels.
Cons:
 - Telephone communication can be intercepted and could reveal your identity
		and/or location.
- It’s not always easy to verify that the person you’re speaking to is who
		they say they are.
Get started:
 Before you get in touch, find the name of the journalist you want to speak to,
	and decide in advance exactly how much you want to tell them about who you are
	and how they can get back to you. The journalist you want may not be available
	when you call, so you may have to leave a message. Be prepared for that.
 If you plan to share documents with us later, look at some of the other
	options in this guide before calling so you can tell the journalist how you’d
	prefer to do that.
 Consider whether or not it is safe to call us from your work or home phone, or
	from any mobile phone that is associated with you. If you buy a pay-as-you-go
	sim card to call us from a new number, think carefully about where and when
	you buy it, and how you pay for it. And remember that mobile phone calls
	disclose the handset ID as well as the sim card.
 After that:
 Call us on one of these numbers:
 - London office: +44 (0)20 3353 2000
- Sydney office: +61 (0)2 8076 8500
- New York office: +1 212 231 7762
- Washington office: +1 202 517 89042
- San Francisco office: +1 415 919 5874
   Postal mail
 Post still has its uses, especially if you want to send us hard copies.
     Pros:
 - If appropriate measures are taken, conventional mail can be a reasonably
		good way to hide who you are.
- If you don’t want to meet a journalist in person, it’s the only reliable way
		to hand over physical objects.
Cons:
 - It’s slow.
- Post can get hijacked or at least scanned in transit.
- Post can get lost.
If you’re not actually being followed it’s fairly unlikely that an envelope or
	small package will get intercepted.
 Get started:
 Stuff can go missing in the post, so consider how bad it would be to lose the
	material you’re planning to send us. Can you make copies?
 Think about whether or not you need to preserve your anonymity. Could the
	posting location give you up? How about the materials and packaging? If you’re
	very worried about the package being traced back to you, post it somewhere
	busy and make sure there is nothing memorable about your or the package’s
	appearance.
 Mail is scanned for dangerous compounds and objects. Don’t include anything
	that could cause problems with delivery. International mail needs a customs
	declaration, and registered mail requires you to provide sender details.

text:
Join as a Guardian Patron
To show your support at a higher level, discover our Patrons programme.
Since 1821 the mission of the Guardian has been to use clarity and imagination to build hope.Katharine Viner, editor-in-chief
Guardian Media Group is a global news organisation that delivers fearless, investigative journalism - giving a voice to the powerless and holding power to account.
Our independent ownership structure means we are entirely free from political and commercial influence. Only our values determine the stories we choose to cover – relentlessly and courageously.
The Guardian’s agenda-setting journalism is underpinned by an independent ownership structure that is different from other global news organisations. It guarantees our journalism and our editor stay independent from any outside influence, whether financial, political or commercial.
In 1936, John Russell Scott — the proprietor of the Manchester Guardian, as it was then known — transferred his family’s stake in the newspaper to a group of trustees. The Scott Trust became the owner of the newspaper, putting in place the independent ownership structure that supports the Guardian to this day.
This independent ownership structure is made up of three key organisations:
This exceptional, if not unique, form of governance for a news publisher ensures that all surplus financial returns are reinvested into our high quality journalism for a global audience rather than benefiting a proprietor or shareholders.
A summary of the governance structure is available here.
The Guardian’s independent, high-impact journalism is powered by its global readership. The Guardian has over 1 million recurring digital supporters from more than 180 countries around the world. It’s thanks to this generosity that we can provide quality, trustworthy reporting that’s open for everyone to read. With no shareholders or billionaire owner, we can investigate and challenge without fear or favour, and amplify stories that need to be told. You can show your support for our work today, in whichever way suits you best.
Choose to give once from just £1, or set up a recurring amount to power our reporting every month or year.
Support usExplore the stories that shaped the week with our magazine, delivered worldwide. From top news picks to insightful opinion pieces and engaging long reads.
The Guardian is globally renowned for its coverage of politics, the environment, science, social justice, sport and culture. Our journalists deliver agenda-setting investigations, breaking live news, compelling opinion writing and the liveliest features, as well as award-winning podcasts, video documentaries and infographics and visuals.
Our investigations have exposed governmental and social failings, including Windrush revelations in the UK, Covid-19, Cambridge Analytica, the Snowden Files, the Panama, Paradise and Pandora Papers, and the Pegasus Project.
Our teams in the UK, US and Australia produce theguardian.com, Guardian Australia, Guardian US, Guardian Weekly, and the Guardian newspaper in the UK.

title: Trump says Benjamin Netanyahu ‘will not be arrested’ if he visits the US
author: Maya Yang
text:
Donald Trump has said Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, “will not be arrested” if he visits the US.
His comments came days after Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, said he was exploring whether his administration could arrest Netanyahu if he visits the city during the UN general assembly in September.
In a Truth Social post on Monday, Trump said Netanyahu, who has been the subject of an international criminal court arrest warrant since November 2024 over alleged war crimes in Gaza, “will not be arrested, in any way, shape, or form while in the United States of America”.
Trump added that Netanyahu is “fighting against the Islamic Republic of Iran” and said “the only ones that should be arrested are the people that led Iran into this unprecedented spiral of death and destruction”.
Speaking to the New York Times on Saturday, Mamdani had said: “I believe that prime minister Netanyahu belongs in The Hague,” where the international criminal court is based, adding: “He’s a war criminal who has been charged by the international criminal court, and what you will find is that is an opinion that is held by many, purely because of what his actions have wrought over these past many years.”
Mamdani, who has described Israel’s war on Gaza as a genocide, also said he is in “an active conversation” with New York City’s law department about his legal authority to direct the New York police to detain Netanyahu. “Whatever the law allows me to do in New York City, that’s what we will do,” he said, adding: “But we won’t be writing our own laws to that end.”
Although the US does not recognize the ICC’s jurisdiction and is not a party to the court, Mamdani pledged during his mayoral campaign last September that he would arrest Netanyahu if he traveled to New York. “It is my desire to ensure that this be a city that stands up for international law,” he said.
Other Israeli leaders, including Yoav Gallant, the country’s former defense minister, as well as the Hamas military leader Mohammed Deif, have also been the subject of ICC arrest warrants. The court accused the Israeli leaders of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, including “starvation as a method of warfare, and … murder, persecution, and other inhumane acts”.

title: ‘It needs to end now’: Democrats urge Trump to halt Iran war after US troop deaths
author: Robert Tait
text:
Democrats have seized on the deaths of three US troops killed in Iranian strikes to urge Donald Trump to urgently reverse his resumption of the war with Iran amid widespread anxiety over climbing casualties.
Even as US forces launched a 10th consecutive wave of attacks against Iranian targets, concern over the deaths of American service personnel threatened to complicate moves to escalate the conflict, which has reignited after he last week walked away from a memorandum of understanding agreed with Iran in June.
The Pentagon released the names of two soldiers killed in a strike on Muwaffaq Salti air base in Jordan on Friday. They were First Lieutenant Tyler James Feehan, 25, of Ewa Beach, Hawaii, and Private Isabella Gonzales, 19, of Carrollton, Texas.
A third member of the armed forces was killed in northern Iraq on Saturday in what US Central Command called a “controlled detonation” of unexploded ordnance. The remains of a possible fourth dead service member were found over the weekend in Jordan.
Chris Murphy, a Democratic senator for Connecticut, accused Trump of having “frighteningly lost control of this war”.
“For those of us who pay attention to the hour-to-hour pace of the Iran War, things are getting very dark very quickly,” he wrote on social media. “The scale of attacks – and threats of escalation – are increasing rapidly.”
The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, declared that the US would not be deterred by the casualties, writing: “Godspeed, heroes. Their sacrifice only stiffens our resolve.”
Iran has vowed to carry out retaliatory strikes against US Gulf allies, which it has branded “collaborators” for providing logistical facilities for strikes on Iranian territory.
In a brief telephone conversation with NewsNation, Trump called the deaths “a very sad thing” and said the service members had died “in service of our country”.
But he faced a chorus of calls from Democrats to step back from his belligerent posture even as Republicans remained supportive.
“The reckless and costly war of choice in Iran has been a disaster for the American people,” wrote Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader in the House of Representatives. “May God continue to watch over our troops who have needlessly been put into harm’s way.”
Mark Warner, the vice-chair of the Senate intelligence committee and a Democrat from Virginia, said there were “hundreds of seriously wounded” US personnel, and added it was “remarkable” that casualty figures had not been higher.
“This is what happens when you start a war of choice. And as a member of the Gang of Eight, I can say unequivocally there was no imminent threat from Iran,” he told CBS’s Face the Nation.
Chris Van Hollen, a Democratic senator from Maryland who has introduced war powers resolutions aimed at ending the Iran campaign unless it receives congressional approval, posted: “This senseless war should never have been started and it needs to end NOW.”
Jeanne Shaheen, the party’s ranking members of the Senate foreign relations committee, called for a return to diplomacy. “The President must negotiate an end to this disastrous war,” she wrote.
And Ted Lieu, a California representative who has also vocally advocated reining in Trump through a war powers resolution, wrote: “We need Republicans to join us in passing the War Powers Resolution NOW.”
The New York Times reported that Iranian forces carried out three strikes against US military targets in Jordan last week before Friday’s deadly attacks that were not disclosed by the Pentagon. The newspaper said the Pentagon also did not reveal “dozens” of casualties and damage inflicted by the earlier strikes.
The latest casualties brought the number of US service members killed since the start of the war on 28 February to at least 17. More than 1,700 Iranian civilians are estimated to have been killed.
The House and Senate have both passed war powers resolutions – requiring the president to ask for congressional approval after 60 days of hostilities – with the aim of restraining Trump. But the White House has contended that there has yet to be 60 days of continuous fighting because the clock stopped after an initial ceasefire in April, which held, shakily, for several weeks.
Republicans, meanwhile, have remained publicly supportive of Trump – despite poll figures showing support for the war and the president’s conduct of it low and sliding. A Washington Post-Ipsos survey showed approval for Trump’s handling of the conflict at 29% – lower than the 33% backing his stewardship of the economy, which has been buffeted by soaring fuel prices caused by the war.
A statement from New Mexico Republicans mourned the fresh casualties but accused Democrats of trying to exploit them for political reasons.
“No matter how much Democrats try to politicize this, President Trump’s actions in Iran have made our country safer from a terrorist regime that has inflicted death and carnage on millions of innocent people around the world, including Americans,” the party said in a statement.
James Comer, a representative from Kentucky and one of Trump’s staunchest supporters on Capitol Hill, told Fox News that a military response to the service members’ deaths was essential.
“I don’t think anyone would prefer that we have any type of military conflict in Iran, but that’s the world that we live in,” he said. “We have to respond, and we have to respond swiftly and with full force, and that’s what President Trump’s doing.”
Riley Moore, a West Virginia Republican, told Fox that the “precision” of the strikes on the Jordanian base suggested Iran was receiving targeting information from Russia or China. He called on the US’s Gulf allies on the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) to help.
“Where do we go from here is also looking at how we’re going to work with those GCC partners in the region because this could tip over … into a regional destabilizing conflict,” he said.

title: Donald Trump to impose 50% tariff on most Canadian goods, White House says
author: Mollie Reilly
text:
Donald Trump is imposing 50% tariffs on most Canadian goods in response to the country retaliating against previous US tariffs, the White House announced on Monday, declaring Canada has unfairly discriminated against American cars, alcohol and dairy products.
The tariffs will hit a wide range of products, the White House said, including wine, hockey sticks and cement. They also include goods previously protected from import taxes under the United States-Mexico-Canada (USMCA) agreement.
The new tariffs will exclude energy products, fish, critical minerals and potash. They also exclude products already subject to tariffs aimed at protecting national security, such as steel and aluminum.
The steep tariffs will probably unleash a new wave of economic chaos, with risks of higher inflation and further fraying of relations between two nations that had been closely woven together before Trump’s return to the White House.
The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, said in a statement that his government had made comprehensive proposals to resolve trade disputes with Washington, asserting that Trump’s past tariffs violated a trade pact between the two countries.
“This trade dispute has raised costs for families, particularly in the US,” he said. “Canada stands ready to engage intensively to address outstanding issues with the US to the mutual benefit of our citizens.”
The White House said the tariffs will go into effect in 30 days, leaving time for possible negotiations between the two countries.
Trump signed three proclamations to launch the tariffs under Section 338 of the 1930 Trade Act. Several Democratic lawmakers last year proposed repealing the section because they said Trump could use it to destabilize the economy.
A White House fact sheet claims Trump is “taking action to hold Canada accountable for its continued discrimination against and unreasonable and unequal treatment of U.S. commerce that has burdened and disadvantaged hardworking Americans”.
Trump claims in the proclamations that Canada discriminates against American automobiles, alcohol and cheese relative to other nations, but his argument rests in large part on retaliatory actions taken by Canada after the US president imposed tariffs on Canada under the pretext that it should do more to stop fentanyl smuggling into the US.
Trump noted in his autos proclamation that Canada maintained, starting in April 2025, a 25% tariff on the imports of US motor vehicles that did not qualify for preferential treatment under the USMCA.
The White House also cited all but two Canadian provinces and territories stopping the sale of US alcoholic beverages, while not imposing similar restrictions on other countries.
Trump also objected to Canada’s treatment of US cheese, saying in his proclamation that Canada discriminates against the US compared with Europe on dairy products.
Trump had threatened last week to impose tariffs due to smoke from devastating wildfires in Canada drifting across large portions of the US.
“We are holding Canada responsible for the fact that they are not properly maintaining their Forests, and Brush therein, and the United States is being unnecessarily invaded by filthy, polluted, and unhealthy air, the quality of which is dangerous, and totally unacceptable!” he wrote on Truth Social.
Trump watched Sunday’s World Cup final with Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister who has previously pushed back on the US president and won the premiership last year on a platform of promising to stand up for Canada.
After the match, Trump told reporters he had raised the issue of wildfire smoke with Carney.
“I told him, I mean, ‘You got to stop these fires from coming in and, you know, poisoning our air. Our air has been poisoned,’” Trump said of their conversation.
A White House official who previewed the new tariffs to reporters said Trump had requested aides explore additional tariffs due to Canadian wildfires harming US air quality, the Associated Press reported.
The Canadian federal government did not immediately comment on Trump’s action, but Doug Ford, the Ontario premier, said he would “never stop fighting to protect Ontario”.
“If these tariffs proceed, Canada should respond tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar,” Ford posted on social media.
Candace Laing, the CEO of the Canadian chamber of commerce, said the Trump administration’s moves were “regrettable” but the two countries needed to use the 30-day window before the tariffs start “to make meaningful progress in advancing formal talks”.
The new taxes on Canadian imports could carry serious political and economic risks for Trump ahead of the November midterm elections for control of Congress. His so-called “liberation day” tariffs last year in April provoked a financial market meltdown over concerns about inflation and a recession, prompting him to walk back the rates for a period of negotiation.
In a 6-3 decision in February, the supreme court ruled that Trump had illegally used emergency executive power to impose his global tariffs, causing the administration to find alternative ways to raise import taxes based on a series of legal authorities.
The US has been forced to pay back $81bn in tariffs so far this fiscal year.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

As the global economy reels from the war he started with Iran in February, Donald Trump stepped up his trade war with Canada on Monday, signing three proclamations to impose 50% tariffs on most imported Canadian goods, citing a provision of a 1930 trade law.
Trump claimed that the tariffs on one of the most important US trade partners, which risk higher inflation in the US, were justified by what he claimed was Canada’s unfair discrimination against American cars, alcohol and dairy products.
A Trump administration official told the Associated Press that Canada was one of the only nations other than China that retaliated against Trump’s previous tariffs and must be held accountable.
Several Democratic lawmakers last year proposed repealing the section of the 1930 Tariff Act used by Trump, fearing that he could use it to destabilize the economy after many of his tariffs were ruled illegal by the US supreme court.
The new 50% tariffs exclude energy products, fish and critical minerals, but include goods that had previously been protected from import taxes by the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA. That 2020 trade pact recently expired and triggered a new set of negotiations that could run until 2036.
There could be more tariffs to come. The official who briefed reporters on the proclamations said that Trump had also asked his aides look into additional tariffs on Canada because its wildfires hurt air quality in the US.
At the World Cup final on Sunday, Trump congratulated players on stage with Canada’s prime minister Mark Carney, a tournament co-host, who has pushed back on Trump’s tariffs and threats to annex Canada.
Trump claims in the proclamations that Canada discriminates against American autos, alcohol and cheese relative to other nations, but his argument rests in large part on retaliatory actions taken by Canada after he imposed a series of tariffs on Canada last year.
Trump’s proclamation on alcohol notes that Canadian provinces and territories halted the purchase and retailing of American alcoholic beverages last year, without noting that action was in response to Trump’s tariffs and taunts about making Canada the 51st US state.
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration on a day when the president imposed new tariffs under an obscure provision of a 1930 law that worsened the Great Depression. Or, as the international trade law expert Scott Lincicome observed: “Tariff Crazytown is officially BACK”.
Here are the latest developments:
As the global economy reels from the war he started with Iran in February, Donald Trump stepped up his trade war with Canada on Monday, signing three proclamations to impose 50% tariffs on most imported Canadian goods, citing a provision of a 1930 trade law.
Canadians across the political spectrum united in anger at Trump. “If these tariffs proceed, Canada should respond tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar,” Ontario premier Doug Ford said. Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, called the tariffs a “direct violation” of the US-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement Trump negotiated. Canada’s Conservatives called the tariffs “another unacceptable and unjustified attack on Canadian workers and our businesses,” adding: “Canadians are not a punching bag.” The leader of Canada’s New Democrats called them “the latest economic grenade thrown over the border by an out of control President who has lost touch with reality.”
Ilya Somin, a professor of law at George Mason University who helped file the successful challenge to Donald Trump’s “liberation day” tariffs, points out, the president’s new 50% tariffs on Canadian imports “are based on Section 338 of the notorious 1930 Smoot-Hawley tariff legislation, which severely exacerbated the Great Depression.”
Nancy Mace, a Republican congresswoman from South Carolina, announced on Monday that she is not entering the race to replace the late senator Lindsey Graham in the snap Republican primary next month.
Trump's legal authority for new Canadian tariffs? Smoot–Hawley.
In a blog post for Reason magazine, Ilya Somin, a professor of law at George Mason University who helped file the successful challenge to Donald Trump’s “liberation day” tariffs, points out, the president’s new 50% tariffs on Canadian imports “are based on Section 338 of the notorious 1930 Smoot-Hawley tariff legislation, which severely exacerbated the Great Depression.”
This novel use of the infamous 1930 law, which, as all viewers of Ferris Bueller’s Day Off know, did not work, is, Somin argues “just the latest of a series of efforts by Trump to usurp congressional tariff authority and impose harmful and dangerous trade restrictions that damage the US economy and poison relations with our allies and trading partners, of which Canada is one of the most important.”
As the economic historian Phil Magness predicted last year, Trump cited Section 338 of the 1930 law to justify his new tariffs on Monday.
As Magness explained in October the authority comes from the Smoot–Hawley Tariff Act, “which turned an economic downturn into a decade-long catastrophe.” Magness went on:
Fearing foreign retaliation against its own protective tariff schedule under Smoot–Hawley, Congress authorized the president to impose tariffs of up to 50 percent on any country that deploys discriminatory trade practices against the United States. Section 338 did not work as intended, as Smoot–Hawley triggered a catastrophic global trade war that brought international commerce to a halt, destroyed the U.S. export market, and thrust us deeper into the Great Depression. Its language remains on the books as a vestigial relic of this notorious law, although its functions have been superseded by later tariff law revisions that imposed more restrictions on the president’s authority.
Canadians across the political spectrum united in anger at Trump's new tariff threat
Canadians across the political spectrum united in anger on Monday to denounce Donald Trump’s new 50% tariffs on imports from Canada.
While the prime minister, Mark Carney, chose his words carefully, opposition parties from his right and left were more forceful in their reaction.
Leaders of Canada’s Conservative party, including the shadow minister for Canada-US relations, Shuv Majumdar, called Trump’s latest tariffs “another unacceptable and unjustified attack on Canadian workers and our businesses,” adding: “Canadians are not a punching bag. Their anxieties about their future have only been deepened. These tariffs must be withdrawn immediately.”
“Fourteen months ago, Prime Minister Mark Carney described the breakdown in our relationship with the United States as the worst economic crisis since the Second World War. He was right,” the generally pro-Trump party leaders continued.
“President Trump is wrong to target Canadian workers and must reverse these tariffs immediately,” they added.
From the opposite end of the spectrum, the leader of Canada’s progressive New Democrats party, Avi Lewis, was even more blunt.
“The announcement of 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods is the latest economic grenade thrown over the border by an out of control President who has lost touch with reality,” Lewis posted on social media. “It is a direct attack on Canadian workers and industries, putting thousands of jobs at risk. And it will drive up costs for American consumers, who like Canadian consumers, are already feeling pain at the pumps and supermarket checkouts because of Trump’s illegal war on Iran.”
“Donald Trump is trying a new, obscure legal basis for this latest attack,” Lewis went on, referring to the legal authority Trump cited, Section 338 of the 1930 Smoot–Hawley Tariff Act that’s never been used before to impose tariffs.
“If these tariffs go ahead, we must be prepared to fight them with counter-tariffs and put every dollar behind supporting workers in affected sectors,” Lewis added. “The Carney government must refrain from more concessions. We are tired of being treated as Trump’s tariff guinea pigs. New Democrats stand with workers, communities and all Canadians in defiance of this newest threat to our economy and sovereignty.
Canadian leader Mark Carney points out Canada 'has merely matched' tariffs imposed by Trump
Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has released a statement in response to threats from Donald Trump to impose new 50% tariffs on Canadian goods in 30 days unless Canada removes barriers on US auto, alcohol and dairy products.
Carney noted that all of the measures imposed by Canada on imports from the US that Trump complained of on Monday were taken in retaliation to previous US tariffs imposed by Trump.
Here is Carney’s full statement:
“Today, the United States administration announced its intention to impose a new 50% tariff on a significant number of Canadian goods.
This is the latest in a series of unilateral U.S. trade actions that began with the U.S. imposing a series of tariffs in direct violation of the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA), the free trade agreement between Canada, the United States, and Mexico.
These include tariffs on the Canadian auto sector, in violation of CUSMA. Canada, as is its right, has merely matched those measures.
More broadly, in response to these measures and threats to Canadian sovereignty, provinces, territories, and Canadians from coast to coast to coast have stood together, taking the necessary actions to support our economy and defend our workers, farmers, businesses, and families.
Recognising that the U.S. has been transforming all of its trade relationships, including those covered under CUSMA, over the past 18 months, Canada has made a series of detailed and comprehensive proposals to resolve this dispute and to modernise CUSMA. We stand ready to intensify those discussions in the coming weeks.
Canada believes in the benefits of free and fair trade, as evidenced by our new government signing more than 20 new economic and security partnerships. This trade dispute has raised costs for families, particularly in the U.S. Canada stands ready to engage intensively to address outstanding issues with the U.S. to the mutual benefit of our citizens.
In all circumstances, Canada will work relentlessly and take any measures necessary to build our strength at home and to support Canadian workers, farmers, businesses, and families.”
As part of the Trump administration’s continuing attack on left-leaning groups, the US state department has listed several activists and organizations as “front groups and fellow travelers” for Cuba, including Hasan Piker and Amazon Labor Union founder Chris Smalls.
In a 100-page report released on Monday, the state department denounces Cuba as the “capital of 21st-century communism”, accusing the Cuban government of carrying out a “campaign of subversion” that has “infiltrated the highest reaches of the US government, recruited and cultivated generations of American activists [and] backed an unprecedented wave of leftwing terrorism on American soil”.
The state department report alleges that the so-called campaign is “designed to turn America against itself” and singles out several left-leaning activists and organizations, including the Democratic Socialists of America, Isra Hirsi – the daughter of Minnesota Democratic representative Ilhan Omar – New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, and journalist Amy Goodman, citing their criticism of US policy toward Cuba or participation in Cuba solidarity movements.
Describing the DSA, of which Mamdani is a member, the report says the organization “serves as a particularly potent illustration of the ideological victory of Cuba’s effort to position itself as the spiritual capital of Third Worldist radicalism”. It accuses the DSA of maintaining a “fierce, almost religious commitment to the cause of the Cuban regime – not because the group is controlled by Cuban agents, per se, but because that commitment is now simply the de facto policy orthodoxy on the American far left”.
Trump has doubled down on similar messaging in recent days, using the term communism at political rallies and presidential engagements alike.
For more than 60 years, the US has maintained a sweeping economic embargo on Cuba, in addition to crippling sanctions imposed by numerous administrations. Despite US claims that its policies are designed to pressure the Cuban government, Havana and many international critics including human rights organizations say they have severely hurt the island’s economy.
US distillers alarmed by Trump's 'further escalation' of trade dispute with Canada
American distillers are worried that Donald Trump’s new 50% tariffs on spirits imported from Canada, announced on Monday and due to go into effect 19 August, could intensify the trade war the president began last year, denting their profits.
“For nearly a year and a half, American spirits have been pulled from store shelves across much of Canada as collateral damage in a broader trade dispute unrelated to our sector, and we appreciate the Administration’s recognition of the significant damage these restrictions have caused U.S. distillers,” Chris Swonger, chief executive of the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, said in a statement on Monday.
“We had hoped, however, that this issue could be resolved without further escalation,” Swonger continued. The new tariff “deepens trade tensions and raises the risk of further retaliation at a time when many U.S. hospitality businesses continue to face financial hardships,” he added, before calling for “policymakers on both sides of the border to pursue a negotiated solution”.
The US trade group makes clear what the Trump administration has not: that Canadians only stopped selling US alcohol last year in response to Trump’s actions. “Canadian provinces removed U.S. spirits from retail shelves in March 2025 in retaliation to U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods,” the council says. As a result, US exports to Canada “fell more than 70% year-over-year from the start of the retaliatory ban in March 2025 through December 2025,” the industry group adds.
The bans have only been lifted in two Canadian provinces: Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Canadian Chamber of Commerce calls for talks before Trump's threatened tariffs go into effect in 30 days
The president of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, Candace Laing, called for talks between the US and Canada before Donald Trump’s newly announced 50% tariffs on Canadian imports take effect in 30 days.
“We knew this would get bumpier before landing. We shared our concerns with the Canadian government about the rising threat Section 338 tariffs posed, given something like this could be coming, “Laing said in a statement, referring to the section of a 1930 US trade law cited by Trump.
”While this is a regrettable escalation by the U.S. Administration, we now have 30 days before this comes into effect,” she added. “Both sides need to use this window to make meaningful progress in advancing formal talks. There are important discussions to get to that will strengthen not threaten our shared prosperity.”
Ontario premier Doug Ford says Canada should retaliate for new Trump tariffs
Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, who leads the Canadian province that has suffered the most from US auto tariffs, called on Canada to retaliate for the new 50% tariffs announced on Monday by Donald Trump, should they go into effect in 30 days.
“I’ll never stop fighting to protect Ontario,” Ford wrote on social media. “If these tariffs proceed, Canada should respond tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar.”
Last year, Ford’s province paid for an anti-tariff television ad that infuriated Trump, because it used parts of a 1987 speech against tariffs given by Ronald Reagan and ran during Major League Baseball World Series games between the Toronto Blue Jays and the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Earlier on Monday, Ford also called Trump’s threat to impose additional tariffs on Canada for failing to prevent wildfire smoke from drifting over the border into the US a “bunch of rubbish.”
Ford pointed out that smoke from wildfires in the US also travels north to Canada.
“With all the assets the US has, and he’s sitting there complaining, why don’t you send up some water bombers?” Ford also asked of Trump. “Why don’t you start helping, like we would help you, in a heartbeat?”
“You should support your neighbors, that’s my message to the president,” Ford added.
Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, said in a statement that the new 50% tariffs on imported Canadian goods imposed on Monday by Donald Trump, under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, was entirely justified.
“While the Administration continues to secure fair and reciprocal trade deals with our trading partners, Canada, unlike other partners and allies, continues to retaliate against the United States for its efforts to rebalance trade and protect U.S. industry in national-security sensitive sectors,” Greer said. “Specifically, Canada has taken U.S. alcohol products off Canadian shelves, given better market access to dairy products from the European Union, and has put a cap on U.S. vehicle exports to Canada from companies reshoring to the United States.”
What Greer did not say is that Canada’s actions, including local bans on selling US alcohol products in some Canadian provinces, were taken in response to tariffs imposed by Trump in the first place, and his threats to annex the country.
Democrats have seized on the deaths of three US troops killed in Iranian strikes to urge Donald Trump to urgently reverse his resumption of the war with Iran amid widespread anxiety over climbing casualties.
Even as US forces launched a 10th consecutive wave of attacks against Iranian targets, concern over the deaths of American service personnel threatened to complicate moves to escalate the conflict, which has reignited after he last week walked away from a memorandum of understanding agreed with Iran in June.
The Pentagon released the names of two soldiers killed in a strike on Muwaffaq Salti air base in Jordan on Friday. They were First Lieutenant Tyler James Feehan, 25, of Ewa Beach, Hawaii, and Private Isabella Gonzales, 19, of Carrollton, Texas.
A third member of the armed forces was killed in northern Iraq on Saturday in what US Central Command called a “controlled detonation” of unexploded ordnance. The remains of a possible fourth dead service member were found over the weekend in Jordan.
Chris Murphy, a Democratic senator for Connecticut, accused Trump of having “frighteningly lost control of this war”.
“For those of us who pay attention to the hour-to-hour pace of the Iran War, things are getting very dark very quickly,” he wrote on social media. “The scale of attacks – and threats of escalation – are increasing rapidly.”
“The reckless and costly war of choice in Iran has been a disaster for the American people,” wrote Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader in the House of Representatives. “May God continue to watch over our troops who have needlessly been put into harm’s way.”
Mark Warner, the vice chair of the Senate intelligence committee and a Democrat from Virginia, said there were “hundreds of seriously wounded” US personnel, and added it was “remarkable” that casualty figures had not been higher.

Donald Trump has said Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, “will not be arrested” if he visits the US.
His comments came days after Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, said he was exploring whether his administration could arrest Netanyahu if he visits the city during the UN general assembly in September.
In a Truth Social post on Monday, Trump said Netanyahu, who has been the subject of an international criminal court arrest warrant since November 2024 over alleged war crimes in Gaza, “will not be arrested, in any way, shape, or form while in the United States of America”.
Trump added that Netanyahu is “fighting against the Islamic Republic of Iran” and said “the only ones that should be arrested are the people that led Iran into this unprecedented spiral of death and destruction”.
Speaking to the New York Times on Saturday, Mamdani had said: “I believe that prime minister Netanyahu belongs in The Hague,” where the international criminal court is based, adding: “He’s a war criminal who has been charged by the international criminal court, and what you will find is that is an opinion that is held by many, purely because of what his actions have wrought over these past many years.”
Mamdani, who has described Israel’s war on Gaza as a genocide, also said he is in “an active conversation” with New York City’s law department about his legal authority to direct the New York police to detain Netanyahu. “Whatever the law allows me to do in New York City, that’s what we will do,” he said, adding: “But we won’t be writing our own laws to that end.”

title: ‘A big job ahead of him’: world leaders congratulate Andy Burnham as he becomes Britain’s PM
author: Jon Henley
text:
World leaders have warmly congratulated Andy Burnham on his entry into 10 Downing Street as Britain’s seventh prime minister in a decade, but international media largely focused on the scale of the challenges awaiting him.
Emmanuel Macron, France’s president, said he hoped for a deeper relationship “in the service of our peoples, and by giving new momentum to the partnership between the UK and the EU” rekindled by Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer.
The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, who spoke with Burnham on Monday evening including about continued support for Ukraine, said Germany and the UK were close partners and he looked forward to working together.
The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said she looked forward to “strengthening the EU-UK partnership”. A “very good first discussion” had revealed a common commitment to “bringing the EU and UK closer and closer”, she later added.
Beyond the diplomatic platitudes, however, media coverage focused on Burnham’s regional persona – and the huge task awaiting him. France’s Public Sénat said the new prime minister came from “the working class of the north of England”.
He had managed to “build an image as an ‘everyman’, appearing without a tie, very often in a T-shirt”, the political TV channel said on its website, standing out as “a politician on the ground, close to everyday concerns”.
Italy’s Corriere della Sera said the UK was experiencing “profound unease, instability and social resentment” and “needs a push” forward, but Burnham’s nationalisation, state intervention and reindustrialisation plans suggested he saw the past as a model.
The UK “appears incapable of imagining and planning for the future and prefers to take refuge in a backward-looking Eden”, it argued, even though the pre-Thatcher years were marked by “energy rationing, rubbish in the streets and IMF bailouts”.
The Irish Times noted that Burnham may be “a breath of fresh air” but the challenges that brought down Starmer – “a budget unable to meet desperately needed demand in defence, housing, welfare, care for the aged, and training for the young” – remained.
The new prime minister, the paper said, would be “hamstrung by a commitment to abide by strict fiscal rules. His instinct may be to tack to the left, but he is already trying to prove that … he will govern from the centre” and the job was “immense”.
In an New York Times essay titled The King of the North Won’t Save Britain, Tom Hazeldine said that with his “northern accent, casual attire and everyman persona”, Burnham “trades on his outsider status, a precious commodity in antipolitical times”.
But, Hazeldine added, a UK that had wanted “a bounce” after Starmer had actually ended up with – in the absence of anything better – “a career Blairite with a northern soul and a Whitehall brain. For the country, it looks a lot like more of the same.”
Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, wished Burnham “a successful tenure”, adding that Italy and the UK were “bound by a deep friendship and a collaboration that, over the years, has grown ever stronger” and she was sure would continue.
Outside the EU, Donald Trump, who had previously described Burnham as “the mayor of a town” and “extremely liberal”, said on Monday night the two had had a “very good conversation” on topics including North Sea oil.
“The Prime Minister has got a big job ahead of him, but he will be able to do it and, of course, the U.S.A. will be there to help!” Trump posted on Truth Social. “The call was interesting, and went very well. I wished Prime Minister Burnham, GOOD LUCK AND GODSPEED!”
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, described the UK as “one of the global leaders”, adding that the two countries’ relationship was “stronger than ever and Kyiv stood “ready to work together in all possible formats”.
Anthony Albanese, the Australian prime minister, said Australia and the UK were “longstanding friends” bound by “deep ties”. He looked forward to strengthening the partnership and promoting “security, resilience and prosperity in the years ahead”.

title: Football, golf … behold the future of world sport: Donald Trump as referee-in-chief | Marina Hyde
author: Marina Hyde
text:
For so many of us around the world, the final scenes of the World Cup were a chance to switch off the TV with an eye-roll and observe mildly: “Well, I think that’s quite enough America for us all for a while now.” And yet: there can and must always be more. It is simply the way of things. If you thought the World Cup being carried on to the pitch ahead of Sunday’s final in some kind of Louis Vuitton sex trunk was the nadir of hysterical trashiness in sport, then simply recall the lesson of the past few years and expand your mind. It can always get trashier.
To the parched fairways of Royal Birkdale, then, the host of this year’s Open Championship, which – yesssssss! – was won by someone other than Bryson DeChambeau or Scottie Scheffler or any of the other radioactively ghastly US golfers you’d cheerfully head-flush in a Mar-a-Lago loo just as long as you could clear the classified documents out of it first. It has now been revealed that, during his heated row over a two-shot penalty he was handed for improving the area for his backswing, DeChambeau has been accused of threatening to call the US president unless it was all resolved in his favour. To repeat: threatening to call Donald Trump.
If you missed this, DeChambeau picked up the penalty for improving the line of his swing, apparently having trodden down some long grass close to his ball on the fifth hole during the second round last Friday. He publicly lost his mind about it, demanded to be driven back to the scene with officials, then returned to the tournament scoring area and reportedly threatened to call Trump. Has a new portal to the dark side opened in sport? Given Trump’s known intervention in the World Cup (of which more shortly), who among us would bet against it?
At time of writing, I had read everything about this sensational escalation, but I still don’t know nearly enough about it. I need every detail. I need everyone involved to reconstruct the entire conversation. I want to know exactly how quickly you might go from “no way did I do any gardening” to “fuck you – patch in the president”. This is a new era of American pant-wetting and I need to understand absolutely everything about its conventions.
Certainly, all I already thought about Bryson DeChambeau has been magnified. If you’re unfamiliar with his work, as well as being a two-time US Open champion, Bryson is a hardcore Mar-a-Lago steak-gobbler who got a shout-out in Trump’s 2024 election victory address, though that was delivered at the Palm Beach Convention Center and not at the latter’s Floridian golf-club residence. (Even so, every time we see those words, the hilarity should strike us anew. The president of the United States of America lives in a golf club. Honestly: I just CAN’T.) Anyway, in the small hours after his victory over Kamala Harris, Trump was very keen to pluck DeChambeau from the sliders queue or the ormolu urinals or wherever and get him up on stage. “Bryson DeChambeau is up here somewhere,” Trump told the cameras. “What happened to Bryson? Where is he? Bryson! He’s hitting balls. He’s on the way?” Eventually, DeChambeau realised there was nothing for it but to climb awkwardly on to the stage.
And yet, where is your orange god now, Bryson? Where was he on Friday, as you seemingly failed to summon him to a faraway British links course having been observed doing a bit of landscaping?
There seems, at present, to be no evidence that Bryson put the call in, and since he flaked out of all media appearances for the tournament, no one has been able to ask if he contacted the president in any other way. We understand, however, that he asked for Trump to be called. Sad. Perhaps the only thing worse than demanding that the president be called over you dicking around with the grass is not having the president called over you dicking around with the grass. And then realising that, in many ways, you got less off Trump than some guy called Folarin Balogun who plays a sport called … hang on, let me get my lorgnette … “soccer”. That would be a lot of perspective for Bryson to absorb on a Friday lunchtime.
The maddest thing about the entire revelation is what it says about how comically debased and politicised sport has been in such short order. Because the thing is, you can totally see it. You can genuinely imagine that the only situation room Trump wouldn’t lose focus in after about 10 minutes is one where he was required to cheat remotely at golf. You can just picture him assembling Pete Hegseth and Marco Rubio and all the other guys with the too-big shoes in the White House situation room, and them huddling round a feed like the photo of the Obama administration watching the Seal team raid that got Osama bin Laden. Only this one is coming from a grass-level camera at Royal Birkdale.
As indicated, we already know the US president cheats at sport for people. Precisely two weeks ago, this column covered the business of him making three phone calls to the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, about the red card and match suspension handed to US striker Balogun. On Sunday, the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, went so far as to boycott the World Cup final over, among other things, Infantino allowing this. The only question, surely, is when the next incident or threat will occur. The floodgates of Whitehousery have been opened, and only the US has the power to shut them.
- 
  Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnist

title: We’ve been desperate for someone to take on Donald Trump. Who knew it would be Coldplay’s Chris Martin? | Simon Price
author: Simon Price
text:
Long before the United States turned the World Cup final into an orgy of pop music and advertising, the signs were already there that this year’s co-hosts should never have been allowed within a thousand miles of the tournament. The garish half-time show curated by Chris Martin of Coldplay seemed to reinforce that – but then came a moment of improbable genius.
I was surprised. The last time America hosted, the problem wasn’t commercial overkill so much as sheer shrugging apathy. I was in New York during USA ’94. Apart from a few flapping banners outside the Nike store, you wouldn’t have known one of the world’s biggest sporting events was taking place. This, in hindsight, was a blessing. Football was allowed to football.
In our rampantly hypercapitalist age, we can only dream of such innocence. In the run-up to its 2026 iteration, co-hosted with Mexico and Canada, the cost to supporters of handing the lion’s share of World Cup games to America’s supersize-everything culture became horribly clear, from obscene ticket prices to price-gouging by local authorities over travel to games, with a $13 train ticket to the MetLife Stadium, venue for the final, hiked to $105. Then came the announcement of so-called “hydration breaks” midway through each half. This was in no way just an excuse for American broadcasters to cram in more advertising. Never again.
On the eve of the tournament, things only got worse. Africa’s top referee, Omar Artan, was refused entry to the States for having the temerity to be Somali. Iraqi striker Aymen Hussein was detained and questioned for seven hours on arrival at O’Hare airport. In a better, saner universe, all 48 competing nations would have boycotted the whole thing in solidarity at this point. But the reaction of the Fifa president Gianni Infantino to any concerns was to tell us to “chill” and “relax”.
Then Fifa announced that this year’s half-time would last 25 minutes – breaking the organisation’s own rules – due to a pop concert along Super Bowl lines. On the day, it began bizarrely: Madonna singing Music on some weird sci-fi Jeep deep in the bowels of the stadium, then emerging from the tunnel flanked, randomly, by Brazil legends Ronaldinho and Ronaldo. The rest of the show was a surreal jumble. Two men exchanging wisecracks, their presence baffling to anyone who doesn’t watch Ted Lasso. The Muppets doing Seven Nation Army. The uncanny valley faces of K-pop megastars BTS looking more like AI creations than flesh and blood. Shakira being Shakira. Wandering minstrel Justin Bieber doing a mournful acoustic ballad called Everything Hallelujah that’s the very antithesis of a bop, planting the crowd’s arses firmly back in their seats.
But then Chris Martin pulled out his Trump card. After footage of Pelé saying the word “love” on the big screens, Coldplay performed a song called Believe in Love, with lines including “Be kind to each other / We’re in this together”, surrounded by dozens of children of multiple ethnicities – the sort of kids Trump’s ICE squads would doubtless deport in a heartbeat – wearing T-shirts with slogans such as “all of us a family”, “I am you and you and you”, and “stars that make a galaxy”. They’re sentiments that would feel trite in more privileged times, but feel radical and essential in 2026. Finally, the sky above the stadium exploded in rainbow smoke above the bleak Sopranos hinterland around the MetLife, an unmistakeable statement of LGBTQ+ solidarity. One can only imagine what the president made of it, behind the bulletproof glass. Martin was, effectively, trolling him.
The US isn’t the only ethically questionable host of a World Cup in history: think of Qatar in 2022 and Russia in 2018, and some of us have memories going all the way back to Argentina in 1978 (and we’ve got Saudi Arabia coming up in 2034). But it’s the first to mess with the fabric of the actual sport, and to relegate football to a sideshow, subservient to the gods of commerce and celebrity.
Ultimately, the Super Bowl is theirs. Let them do what they want with that. Football is ours, everyone’s. Here’s hoping, naively, that some future incarnation of Fifa will consign Trump and Infantino’s venal and vulgar innovations to the dustbin. In his own way, Chris Martin has shown us how.
- 
  Simon Price is a music journalist and author
