title: Trump’s HIV funding cuts having ‘severe and devastating’ impact around the world
author: Kat Lay
text:
No part of the United States’ anti-HIV programme has escaped unscathed from Donald Trump’s funding cuts, despite pledges from the administration to protect care that saved lives around the world, a new report has found.
Funding cuts to the President’s Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar) have caused “severe and devastating” disruption globally, with thousands of staff laid off and many clinics closed, according to research being presented next week at the 26th International Aids Conference in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. It warns that changes in US policy risk reversing progress in the fight against HIV/Aids.
Organisations still in receipt of US funding are also changing what they do to comply with the Trump administration’s policies targeting diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives, reproductive rights and the provision of gender-affirming care, researchers found.
Elise Lankiewicz, from the Aids research foundation Amfar and co-lead author of its Pepfar Pulse report, said: “Disruption was incredibly widespread. No part of the programme really escaped unscathed – and that includes areas of the programme that this administration intended to protect.”
Pepfar is credited with saving more than 26 million lives and changing the trajectory of the HIV epidemic since it was set up in 2003 during George W Bush’s presidency.
It works through partner organisations around the world, who find people at risk and offer them testing for HIV, protection against the virus, such as condoms or medicines, and treatment if needed.
However, many of its grants were abruptly withdrawn by the Trump administration in 2025 – more than half had been managed via USAID, the agency dissolved by Trump in July 2025. A waiver that was issued months before, in February 2025, theoretically allowed programmes providing life-saving treatment or preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission to continue.
“The reality is it’s incredibly hard to cut one award without there being ripple effects throughout the system,” said Lankiewicz.
Amfar surveyed 166 organisations across 46 countries that had been due to receive Pepfar funding in 2025. More than half of the respondents had at least one terminated award, resulting in more than 1,700 closed clinics, drop-in centres or other sites. Prevention services were particularly hard hit. More than 16,000 full-time staff lost their jobs.
Almost two-thirds of organisations providing services to prevent mother-to-child HIV transmission reported disruption, with a fifth ending services entirely. A fifth of organisations providing HIV care and treatment stopped at least one service, the researchers found. Many said they were unable to obtain supplies of laboratory commodities, condoms or drugs.
Five surveyed organisations had closed; three as a direct result of losing Pepfar funding. However, the researchers said: “This is likely a significant under-count, since closed organisations would no longer have active email accounts by which to receive the survey.”
Services for the key populations of people most vulnerable to HIV – such as gay or transgender people, injectable drug users or sex workers – were most likely to have ended.
Almost four out of five respondents said they had been asked to restrict their work to comply with an additional US policy – typically anti-DEI executive orders, but also an expanded “global gag rule”, said Lankiewicz.
“They made pretty dramatic shifts to their programming to align with these new policies,” she said, adding that this included ending services tailored to specific people such as sex workers, as well as support for victims of gender-based violence.
Greg Millett, a member of the study team, said: “Until now, much of the discussion about the impact of recent Pepfar disruptions has relied on projections and modelling. This study provides some of the first real-world data.”
The results mirror earlier analysis of US government data, which showed a severe drop in numbers of frontline health workers, HIV diagnoses and prevention programmes.
“These disruptions threaten to reverse progress toward controlling the HIV epidemic,” Millett told a press briefing ahead of the Aids 2026 conference, which is organised by the International Aids Society.

title: Seth Meyers on Trump at the World Cup: ‘They’re going to have to sage the stadium’
author: Guardian staff reporter
text:
On Monday night, Seth Meyers discussed Donald Trump getting booed at this weekend’s World Cup final, confusion over the Iran war and the mystery surrounding Mitch McConnell’s health.
On his NBC show, Meyers pointed out the irony of the US president celebrating with the Spanish football team after they won the World Cup.
“Lately he’s [been] in an especially tense relationship with Spain,” the host said. “He’s mad at them because they won’t support his pointless war with Iran.
In a meeting with the Nato secretary general earlier this month, Trump called Spain a “terrible partner in Nato”, adding: “I don’t want anything to do with Spain. Cut off all trade with Spain, please.”
After Spain’s victory at the Fifa tournament on Sunday, Trump stepped on to the podium alongside the team at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium and cheered them on.
“If you’re surprised he’s up there, you forgot the first rule of Trump, which is: everything goes out of the window if gold is around.
“Less than a month ago he said no more visits from Spain, and now Spain is in America holding the world’s most coveted trophy while Trump stands next to them like Forrest Gump during the history montage.”
Meyers pointed out that Trump was not supposed to be up there with the winners, with the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, running over and attempting to guide Trump off the podium.
“The head of the most corrupt organization on Earth was, like, ‘This is a bad look,’” laughed Meyers.
“But Trump insisted on standing there, either because he wanted the attention or he forgot where he was because he’s 80 and his brain is smoother than a soccer ball.”
Spain’s captain, Rodrigo Hernández Cascante, better known as Rodri, also seemed to be trying to usher Trump offstage. “OK grandpa, time for bed!” quipped Meyers.
“It’s like being at a house party in high school, getting ready to cheer a buddy on for a keg stand, and then your weirdest neighbor walks into the house,” said the host.
Trump was booed at the football match with the crowd shouting and jeering as he stepped on to the field for the trophy presentation after the game.
“At this point, I’m guessing Trump’s staff tries to make him feel better by telling him he’s just being followed around by ghosts,” Meyers said, before impersonating an aide: “‘Mr President, remember that no one’s booing you: that’s just Mitch McConnell saying hello.’
“I’m just kidding, Mitch McConnell is definitely alive,” he continued. “They always make you stay in the hospital an extra week after you put your jeans on.
“It sucks that he had to show up and put his stink on another event that was otherwise bringing New Yorkers together, Meyers said, referencing Trump’s recent appearance at the NBA finals. “They’re gonna have to sage MetLife Stadium to get the hex out.”
Ahead of the game, Trump predicted an Argentina victory saying that it was hard to bet against Lionel Messi.
“Trump’s sports curse strikes again,” said Meyers. “He goes to the NBA finals, the Knicks lose. He intervenes to get a red card overturned, USA loses.
“He says you can’t bet against Messi, Argentina loses. He owned a USFL team, and the whole fucking league folded. He’s a sports reaper.”
Trump continues to claim that the US has won the war in Iran despite the conflict continuing in the region.
“Obviously, the opposite is happening,” Meyers said. “The Iran war only seems to be spiralling further out of control.”
Trump has claimed 38 times that the war is over, but also said last week that Iran would be defeated soon. “Which is a weird thing to say about a country you claim has already been defeated.”

title: Trump defends 50% tariffs on Canada, saying ‘they need us to survive’
author: Shrai Popat
text:
Donald Trump has defended his new 50% tariffs on most Canadian goods, claiming the country cannot survive without the US.
The White House announced the sweeping round of import duties – due to come into effect next month – on Monday, igniting fresh tensions between Washington and Ottawa.
Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, said his country was “united” in the face of such threats. He spoke with Trump earlier on Tuesday.
“Canada has been very, very tough on us over the years, for many years, and no other president’s done anything about it,” the US president said in the Oval Office. “In all fairness to them, they need us to survive. Without us, there’s no way they can survive.”
Earlier this week, the White House said that the new levies were because Canada has unfairly discriminated against US cars, alcohol and dairy products. The tariffs will go into effect in 30 days, leaving time for possible discussions between the two countries.
Carney told reporters: “We agreed to intensify negotiations in the coming weeks, and the team and myself look forward to doing that.”
The tariffs will hit a wide range of products, the White House said, including wine, hockey sticks and cement. They also include goods previously protected from import taxes under the United States-Mexico-Canada (USMCA) agreement.
Trump told members of the press that the latest round of tariffs was not in response to the Canadian wildfire smoke that spread across North America last week.
On Friday, Trump blasted Canada for its response to the persistent wildfires and the smoke that affected about 109 million people across the midwest, mid-Atlantic and north-east.
“The cost is incalculable!” Trump raged on social media. “This is Willful Negligence, and becoming a yearly occurrence, costing the United States Billions of Dollars, which cost of this pollution must of necessity be added to the TARIFFS Canada is currently paying.”
However, the president told reporters on Tuesday that his administration was looking at those tariffs “separately”.

title: Trump to allow direct US flights to Lebanon after 41-year halt
author: Associated Press; Guardian staff reporter
text:
Donald Trump said on Tuesday he would allow American carriers to resume direct flights to Lebanon more than 40 years after the US suspended the route.
Direct flights between the US and Lebanon were suspended in 1985 by Ronald Reagan’s administration following the hijacking of TWA flight 847.
“I am hereby directing my Administration to allow all U.S. airline carriers to fly directly to Lebanon so that Americans can easily visit this beautiful land,” Trump said in a social media post after meeting with the Lebanese president, Joseph Aoun.
During the meeting with Aoun, Trump pledged to help Lebanon “a lot”. Aoun came to Washington to push for long-term calm after months of war between Israel and the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group.
The US has pushed for peace in Lebanon but has been distracted by a new round of escalation in Iran, which has destabilized much of the Middle East. Trump recently said he had little interest in talks with Iran’s leader to end the war – at least for now.
Lebanon and Israel have held rare direct talks mediated by Washington. Aoun’s White House visit was the first by a Lebanese president since 2009.
“It’s been a very badly treated place and country and we’re going to have it properly treated and treated with the respect it deserves,” Trump told Aoun during the White House meeting, which wrapped up the Lebanese leader’s four-day visit to Washington.
“We’re gonna help it a lot,” he said, without giving concrete details.
Lebanon hopes the Washington talks result in Israeli troops withdrawing from large parts of southern Lebanon they currently occupy, and the Lebanese military receiving support to assert full control in areas where Hezbollah militants had held sway.
Trump said of Israel’s army fully withdrawing from Lebanon: “They’re in the process of doing that. They’re in the process of redeploying.” He did not elaborate.
Aoun told Trump: “Your vision is peace.” He called it Trump’s “legacy”.

title: Trump must divulge financial details about businesses in $10bn BBC lawsuit
author: Roque Planas
text:
Donald Trump must divulge detailed financial information from his many businesses as part of his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the British Broadcasting Corporation, a federal judge ruled during a discovery hearing on Tuesday, according to news reports.
The ruling by US magistrate judge Enjoliqué Lett could open a unique window into the hundreds of businesses owned by Trump’s family trust. It also highlights a potential drawback for Trump’s strategy of bludgeoning critical media with multibillion-dollar lawsuits.
Trump filed a defamation lawsuit late last year seeking $10bn in damages over a 2024 documentary called “Trump, A Second Chance,” which features a scene of the speech he made before his supporters attacked the US Capitol on 6 January 2021. The scene splices lines together to make it appear that Trump directly urged his supporters to attack. The BBC apologized to Trump last year for the misleading edit, but has argued the president’s defamation claims have no merit.
Lett is also allowing the BBC to subpoena dozens of members of Trump’s inner circle, according to Bloomberg News, in an effort to find evidence of the president’s thoughts and intentions on January 6. Those subpoenas will target Trump family members and key advisers, including Donald Trump Jr, Steve Bannon and Stephen Miller.
Trump’s legal team is likely to appeal Tuesday’s decision.
Trump’s lawyers are also trying to dodge the forced release of his financial records by limiting the scope of the lawsuit. Alejandro Brito, a Trump lawyer, told Lett on Tuesday that he intends to amend the current complaint, according to Politico. The amended complaint will say the documentary only caused reputational damage, rather than undermining his businesses, making the financial disclosures unnecessary.
But for now, the BBC can move forward with requests for Trump’s financial records. The BBC aims to argue that Trump’s wealth skyrocketed since the documentary aired, contradicting the claim that the documentary undermined his businesses.
The White House did not immediately return the Guardian’s request for comment.

title: Canada cancels joint bridge-opening celebration with US amid trade tensions
author: Associated Press; Guardian staff reporter
text:
A planned joint US-Canada ceremony Friday celebrating the opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge connecting Detroit and Windsor, Ontario, is no longer expected to take place after Donald Trump announced a 50% tariff on most Canadian goods.
In announcing the tariffs, the president accused Canada of unfairly discriminating against US automobiles, alcohol and dairy products, escalating tensions with one of the United States’ closest allies.
“In light of trade action threatened by the United States earlier this week, it would be inappropriate to proceed with a celebratory event between the two countries,” said Jenna Ghassabeh, a spokesperson for Canadian Infrastructure Minister Gregor Robertson, in an emailed statement.
The move came after US and Canadian officials reached an agreement earlier this month to open the Gordie Howe International Bridge after delays tied to disagreements between the two countries.
Canada now plans to hold its own ceremony on Friday. It is now unclear whether the United States will hold a separate ceremony.
Two US officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations said they still expect the bridge to open to traffic 27 July but are less certain than they were before.
“We remain committed to opening the bridge on July 27th, and to celebrating this milestone among Canadians on July 24th,” said Ghassabeh.
The 1.5-mile-long (2.4-kilometer-long) bridge spans the Detroit River and connects Detroit with Windsor. A ribbon-cutting ceremony had initially been scheduled for 12 June but was abruptly postponed after officials said the United States and Canada were still working to resolve “outstanding issues”.
Canada financed construction of the bridge under an agreement allowing it to recover the cost through toll revenue. The Trump administration had sought changes to that arrangement.
The project, negotiated under former Michigan govenor Rick Snyder, has been under construction since 2018 and cost nearly $4.4bn.
The bridge is named after Canadian hockey great Gordie Howe, who spent 25 seasons with the Detroit Red Wings. It is expected to become another major economic artery between Canada and the United States.
In February, Trump demanded in a social media post that Canada give the US government at least half ownership of the bridge and agree to other unspecified demands, part of his broader clashes with Canada over trade.
Those tensions resurfaced this week. The White House said the tariffs would take effect in 30 days, leaving time for negotiations. Trump has previously delayed or backed away from some threatened import taxes.
Canadian prime minister Mark Carney said in a statement about the tariffs that his government believes in the “benefits of free and fair trade” and remains prepared to negotiate with the Trump administration.
The tariffs could escalate into a broader trade war as Canada weighs how to respond.
“If these tariffs proceed, Canada should respond tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar,” Ontario premier Doug Ford posted on social media.

title: What is Pickaxe Mountain, Iran’s underground nuclear facility Trump is threatening to attack?
author: Agencies; Guardian staff reporter
text:
With the conflict between the US and Iran facing its most sustained outbreak of violence since a ceasefire was agreed in April, Donald Trump has returned to threatening Iranian nuclear sites.
The current run of US strikes is aimed at forcing Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz, but in comments on Tuesday, the president said that his administration remained committed to stopping Iran obtaining a nuclear weapon, and reiterated threats against a site linked to the country’s nuclear programme.
Referring to Pickaxe Mountain – known in Iran as Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La, a fortified underground site near one of the country’s primary nuclear enrichment facilities – Trump told reporters that the military would be “hitting that area pretty soon, and very heavily”.
Here’s what we know about Pickaxe Mountain.
Where is Pickaxe Mountain?
Pickaxe Mountain is located 220km (140 miles) south of Tehran and 2km (1.2 miles) from the Natanz nuclear facility. The Natanz site, where two of Iran’s uranium enrichment plants are located, has been bombed before; during the war started by the US and Israel on 28 February, and during the 12-day war of 2025.
Little is known about the complex located inside the mountain, but experts believe it is still under construction and estimate it is buried almost 100 metres inside the mountain.
The facility at Pickaxe Mountain was not targeted in either of the rounds of US-Israeli strikes in 2025 and 2026, according to the Institute for Science and International Security (ISIS), a US-based thinktank focused on nuclear non-proliferation.
What is the history of Pickaxe Mountain?
Construction of the facility at Pickaxe Mountain began in 2020, according to the ISIS thinktank, after what Iranian authorities reported at the time as an explosion caused by an act of sabotage at the Natanz facility.
Iran said at the time the Natanz sabotage had caused significant damage, and in September of that year, Iran’s then nuclear chief, Ali Akbar Salehi, said the country had started building a “modern, larger and more comprehensive hall in all dimensions in the heart of the mountain near Natanz” for making advanced centrifuges. These machines spin uranium at high speeds to enrich it and produce nuclear fuel.
Rafael Grossi, the chief of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), said in March that Iran had previously announced its intention to have nuclear activity at Pickaxe Mountain.
“This was part of their quite systematic intention to put their most sensitive facilities underground,” he said.
What has Iran built at Pickaxe Mountain?
The ISIS thinktank, which has analysed satellite imagery of the site, says it features two pairs of entrances and that a security wall around the facility was recently completed.
Since the US and Israel began launching strikes, a pair of eastern tunnel portal entrances has been hardened and partially backfilled to obstruct ground vehicle access, but they have not been sealed fully, the thinktank reports.
Sam Lair, a fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, who also reviewed recent satellite imagery of the site, told Reuters that increasing the strength of the tunnel entrances would complicate “targeting with penetrating munitions like bunker busters”.
Is Pickaxe Mountain functioning and what could it be used for?
Trump’s threats to target the mountain earlier this month also included an admission from the president that US intelligence sees “no activity there”.
“They’re not doing well with their nuclear situation. Every time we hear about it, we blow it up. So they don’t like talking about it. But we’ll probably give Pickaxe a shot relatively soon,” he said.
The ISIS thintank, in its report, said its assessment “is that the facility is not yet operational, but construction continues”, and that it was unclear when it could be operational, based on satellite imagery alone.
The thinktank says it is also unclear if Iran still plans on installing a large-scale assembly facility there.
“Nonetheless, if Iran starts to rebuild its centrifuge manufacturing capability, it could plan to install a smaller centrifuge assembly facility in Pickaxe Mountain able to serve a nuclear weapons program,” the ISIS report said.
How might Pickaxe Mountain be attacked?
Experts assess the deeply buried complex as being beyond the reach of the most powerful bunker buster bombs in the US arsenal. Aerial attacks also carry a degree of uncertainty, because assessing their effectiveness can be difficult without on-the-ground intelligence. A Pentagon report issued after the US launched strikes on Iran’s nuclear sites in 2025 said the damage caused likely set back the nuclear program by one to two years, but that conclusion came with a large amount of uncertainty.
The ISIS thinktank said the site “would be more suitable for ground forces to attack or sabotage … however, vulnerabilities may also exist that can be exploited by deep earth penetrating weapons via aerial attacks.”
The deployment of ground operations have so far been a red line for Trump and there has been no suggestion that he is any closer to considering such a move, even after the recent escalation between the US and Iran.
Lair said: “We can infer that there are ongoing activities at Pickaxe Mountain the Iranians wish to continue, but are still concerned enough about a potential attack that they are taking steps to bolster their defences.”
With Reuters

title: Trump announces new tariffs on generic drugs to take effect in 2028 – as it happened
author: Shrai Popat; Tom Ambrose; Maya Yang; Robert Mackey; Chris Stein; Melody Schreiber; Kat Lay; Alice Speri; Robert Tait
text:
Trump announces still more tariffs, this time on generic drugs
Donald Trump announced a new package of tariffs on Tuesday, this time on generic drugs made overseas, to begin in 2028.
The announcement, in a social media post, came just three months after the president issued a proclamation saying that generic pharmaceuticals “are not subject to tariffs at this time” but that decision “will be reassessed in one year.”
Trump’s latest head-spinning reversal on tariff policy means, he said, that generic drugs will continue to be imported tariff-free until 1 August 2028, when a 100% tariff would be imposed “for a one year period of time, and 200% thereafter.” The goal of the policy, Trump said, was to coerce drug makers into building plants in the United States.
Trump did not state what legal authority he was claiming to impose future tariffs on generic drugs, particularly the projected 200% tariff which would come into effect in August 2029, six months after the end of his final term.
This brings our live coverage of the second Trump administration to an end for the day, with just 913 more to come. Here are the latest developments:
As he wages war on Iran to prevent that country from enriching uranium, Donald Trump has reportedly approved a deal with Saudi Arabia to have US firms build a civilian nuclear energy program in the kingdom, which could include a uranium enrichment facility, US officials told the Wall Street Journal. The deal, which the administration plans to submit to Congress in the coming days, does not include safeguards to stop materials being used in nuclear weapons programs, Reuters reports.
The US-Israeli war on Iran has cost the Pentagon $37.5bn so far, defense secretary Pete Hegseth told the Senate Appropriations Committee on Tuesday.

The Senate intelligence committee on Tuesday advanced the nomination of Jay Clayton to serve as the US intelligence director, despite criticism from Democrats.
The Trump administration paused more than $1bn in Medicaid funding to California and Minnesota, two states run by elected Democrats, citing “suspected fraud and noncompliance”.
Trump agrees to provide Saudi Arabia with nuclear enrichment infrastructure - reports
As he wages war on Iran to prevent that country from enriching uranium, Donald Trump has reportedly approved a deal with Saudi Arabia to have US firms build a civilian nuclear energy program in the kingdom, which could include a uranium enrichment facility, US officials told the Wall Street Journal.
The deal, which the administration plans to submit to Congress in the coming days, does not include safeguards to prevent the uranium from being used to make nuclear weapons, Reuters reports.
The 30-year deal is estimated to be worth tens of billions of dollars, the Journal reports.
The agreement could be signed as soon as Wednesday by the US energy secretary , Chris Wright, and the Saudi energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman.
The two men signed a preliminary agreement in Riyadh last year.
Trump has previously scoffed at the idea that Iran might need or want to enrich uranium for peaceful civilian purposes, including energy.
Mamdani says New York City does not have the legal authority to arrest Netanyahu for war crimes, but calls on federal government to do so
“Benjamin Netanyahu is a war criminal, the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people,” New York mayor Zohran Mamdani said on Tuesday in a video statement in which he called the International Criminal Court warrant for the Israeli prime minister’s arrest justified but admitted that he lacks the legal authority to enforce it.
“My administration has reviewed every avenue available under applicable law to determine whether New York City could execute the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant if Benjamin Netanyahu came here,” Mamdani said. “It is clear that we do not have the independent legal authority to enforce this warrant.”
“The federal government, however, does— and I call on them to join the ICC and execute this warrant,” the mayor added, one day after Donald Trump rejected the idea, writing on social media: “Benjamin Netanyahu will not be arrested, in any way, shape, or form, while in the United States of America.”
“Benjamin Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City, nor is any other war criminal at large,” Mamdani said.
Netanyahu is expected to travel to New York in September to address the United Nations general assembly.
For many years, the Israeli prime minister has made the supposed threat posed by Iran’s nuclear enrichment program the focus of his annual speech to the UN. Last year, scores of delegates walked out of the hall before he could begin.
Unlike 125 other countries, the United States is not a state party to the Rome Statute, which established the ICC, and so is not obligated to arrest indicted war crimes suspects.
Last week, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, announced “a sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court to U.S. sovereignty” and promised to “systematically disable the ICC’s ability to operate”.
The arrest of accused war crimes suspects has tested notions of sovereignty in international law in the past.
In 1998, the former Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet was arrested while visiting London on the orders of the Spanish judge Baltasar Garzón who sought Pinochet’s extradition to Spain to face charges of genocide, terrorism and torture. Pinochet was was detained for 16 months before the UK’s home secretary decide that he was too ill to stand trial and allowed him to return home on compassionate grounds.
In 1960, Adolf Eichmann, the Nazi official who organized the deportation of millions of European Jews to death camps, was secretly arrested by Israeli commandos in Argentina, where he had been living under an assumed name. Rather than request his extradition from an Argentine government that had given refuge to prominent Nazis, the Israeli snatch team held Eichmann for 10 days and smuggled him out of the country disguised as an El Al flight attendant to stand trial in Jerusalem.
As Donald Trump announces new tariffs daily, leading one sober trade expert to observe, “Tariff Crazytown is officially BACK”, Democratic lawmakers are lining up to promise to repeal the Trump tariffs as soon as they regain control of Congress.
“Democrats will flip the House. And on Day 1 of next term, Democrats will introduce legislation to repeal trump’s disastrous tariffs. And we will pass it,” congressman Ted Lieu, a California Democrat, wrote after Trump imposed 50% tariffs on a range of goods from Canada on Monday, citing Section 338 of the disastrous Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 as his legal authority.
“Donald Trump has abused every trade authority at his disposal, and he is now excavating a law from the Great Depression to once again impose vast, unilateral tariffs on products from one of our closest allies and trading partners,” senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, said in a statement. “This is yet another shakedown that will raise the cost-of-living for Americans, their families, and small businesses across the country. Trump cannot be trusted with tariff authority, and I will be introducing a bill very soon to rein him in and put Congress back in the driver’s seat.”
The Trade Act of 1930, generally known as the Smoot-Hawley tariff, lost its standing as the worst trade policy action in US history when Donald Trump imposed his “Liberation Day” tariffs in April 2025. But Smoot-Hawley was widely recognized as a terrible mistake soon after its passage, as it provoked widespread retaliation and contributed to the downward spiral of world trade that accompanied and reinforced the Great Depression. …
Yesterday the Trump administration invoked an obscure and never-before-used provision of Smoot-Hawley — Section 338 — to impose 50 percent tariffs on a wide range of Canadian goods. …
Whatever the real motivation for these new tariffs, they are almost surely illegal. They are definitely a violation of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade agreement, a revision of NAFTA negotiated and signed by Trump himself during his first term …
So these latest actions confirm what most people around the world, from the European Commission to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard, have already figured out: a deal with Donald Trump lasts only until he feels like breaking it.

Trump did not state what legal authority he was claiming to impose future tariffs on generic drugs, particularly the projected 200% tariff which would come into effect in August 2029, six months after the end of his final term.
Iran war has cost $37.5bn so far, Hegseth tells Senate
The US-Israeli war on Iran has cost the Pentagon $37.5bn so far, defense secretary Pete Hegseth told the Senate Appropriations Committee on Tuesday.
At the Senate hearing, which has now concluded, senator Dick Durbin, an Illinois Democrat, asked Hegseth to explain why the Pentagon was asking Congress for an additional $67bn to pay for the war Trump started on 28 February when “the Department of Defense still has $75bn in unobligated funding from last year’s reconciliation package”.
“That 75,” Hegseth replied, “there’s plans and designs on that part of the rebuild of our military which had to be undertaken.”
Hegseth then launched into a deeply partisan attack on his predecessor, Lloyd Austin, the retired army general, for supposedly pursuing “woke priorities” instead of military readiness.
“I don’t know what Lloyd Austin did for four years, I really don’t,” he went on. “The amount of neglect, the amount of stale thinking and bureaucracy proceed staggering when we took over.”
“Let me interrupt your speech for a minute, Mr Secretary,” Durbin cut in.
“You estimated at one point that the cost of the war in Iran was $29bn, but then added a caveat that there was a replacement of munitions, for example. Do you have a new estimate about what the war has cost us so far in this the fifth month of the first year of this war in Iran?” the senator asked.
“Senator, the estimate we have, as of today, is $37.5bn,” Hegseth answered.
Pressed further by Durbin, Hegseth said that was the estimated cost of the war on Iran through the end of the US government’s financial year on 30 September.
Voting rights expert calls New Jersey voter registration glitch 'miniscule'
The White House called on Tuesday for the House and Senate to pass the Republican SAVE America Act, which would require proof of citizenship to register to vote, and photo ID to cast a ballot, after New Jersey’s governor, Mikie Sherrill, revealed that a computer software error in the state’s automatic voter registration system for licensed drivers mistakenly registered about 6,600 people who identified themselves as non-US citizens in 2023 and 2024.
According to Sherrill, who was not in office at the time, “fewer than 400 individuals who were newly registered for the first time because of the error voted. They were registered as Democrats, Republicans and Unaffiliated voters and were scattered across the state.”
David Becker, a voting rights expert who leads the nonprofit Center for Election Innovation & Research, put the size of the glitch into context in a statement sent to reporters.
“While administrative errors such as New Jersey’s do infrequently occur, they are very rare and affect a very small fraction of voters. The states entrusted to run our elections are best positioned to detect and correct these errors, as they have access to substantially better data than the federal government,” Becker said.
“As CEIR’s own research affirms, noncitizen registration remains extremely rare, and noncitizen voting is infinitesimally rare. In this case, the number of wrongful registrations represents a miniscule fraction, roughly 0.1%, of New Jersey’s total active voter registration records in 2024,” he continued.
“The number of potential ballots cast from those incorrect registrations would represent roughly 0.009% of all ballots cast in New Jersey’s 2024 general election, when Kamala Harris defeated President Trump by more than 250,000 votes,” Becker added. “Joe Biden actually defeated Trump by a margin three times as large before this error took place.”
Hegseth refuses to say that US military has ability to destroy Iranian facility buried beneath Pickaxe mountain
At the ongoing Senate Appropriations Committee hearing, senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, pressed US defense secretary Pete Hegseth to say whether the US military could bomb a fortified underground site linked to Iran’s nuclear program known as Pickaxe mountain, which the US has not yet targeted.
“We need straight answers,” Kennedy said with some exasperation. “Do we have the ability to destroy whatever is underneath Pickaxe mountain?”
“Senator, a lot of our capabilities are classified, but if anybody in the world can reach anything on God’s given, God’s green Earth, it’s the United States military,” Hegseth replied.
Kennedy’s question was perhaps triggered by reports that experts suggest the site is beyond the reach of the most powerful bunker buster bombs in the US arsenal.
Donald Trump was asked by a reporter earlier on Tuesday if he believes an Israeli intelligence assessment that Iran has moved nuclear centrifuges into tunnels deep inside the mountain, called Kolang Gaz La in Persian, which is about a mile from Iran’s badly damaged Natanz uranium enrichment facility.
“I think that they may have; we don’t have it on record,” Trump replied, before veering into a digression to cast the speculation about the mountain as possibly flawed reporting from news outlets. “All we do is read the fake news, you know, we see… the news is so wrong so many times, so you know, maybe this one they have right.”
“It doesn’t mean anything unless they have the material. You’re talking about the centrifuges,” Trump added. “We follow the material, that’s where the action is, and we’ll be hitting that area very, probably pretty soon and very heavily.”
According to the nonpartisan Institute for Science and International Security think tank in Washington, this site was “not visibly attacked” by US bombers in 2025, when US bombers dropped two two GBU-57 bunker buster bombs on the nearby nuclear facility at Natanz.
“Iran announced in 2020 that the purpose of the Pickaxe tunnel complex is to hold an advanced centrifuge assembly facility that can produce several thousand centrifuges a year,” the institute reported last year. “In addition, based on the estimated size of the underground halls, the Institute several years ago assessed that site could also hold a centrifuge enrichment facility.”
The Senate intelligence committee on Tuesday advanced the nomination of Jay Clayton to serve as the US intelligence director, despite criticism from Democrats.
Donald Trump had nominated Clayton, now the top federal prosecutor in the southern district of New York, for the role of the director of national intelligence (DNI) last month after the departure of Tulsi Gabbard.
Intelligence committee members questioned Clayton at a hearing last week, and its Republican chair, Tom Cotton, announced that it had reported his nomination favorably by a 9-8 vote, teeing him up for a future vote on his confirmation by the full Senate.
“Jay Clayton is a highly qualified nominee with a deep experience combatting a wide range of national security threats,” Cotton said in a statement.
“I’m pleased that the Senate Intelligence Committee voted to advance his nomination to be Director of National Intelligence,” he added.
Cotton did not provide a breakdown of how lawmakers voted. The committee is composed of nine Republicans and eight Democrats, and a spokesperson for the Democratic vice-chair, Mark Warner, said he had opposed the nomination.
At his hearing last week, members of the Democratic minority criticized Clayton, a former Wall Street attorney who served as chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), for refusing to say that Joe Biden won the 2020 election. He also faced questions about previous statements he made echoing Trump’s claim that US elections have been marred by fraud, and concerns about politicization at the office of the DNI, which serves to coordinate the nation’s intelligence agencies.
'Air power's got limits' top US military commander says when pressed on whether strikes on Iran can end war
At the Senate Appropriations Committee hearing, Dan Caine, the chairman of the joint chiefs of staff, was asked by senator Jack Reed, a Rhode Island Democrat and veteran who previously taught economics and international relations at West Point, whether Iran can be deterred and defeated by “air strikes alone”.
“I think, academically, as you look across the totality of history, air power’s got limits, and we always have to be mindful of those,” Caine responded.
He went on to say that the US is combing military power with “the totality of the diplomatic, informational and economic” measures. “There’s a loot of that work going on, sir,” Trump’s hand-picked joint chiefs chair added.
Reed then asked if Caine anticipates the next step in escalation: ground troops.
“Sir, I think it would be unhelpful for me to opine on hypotheticals,” Caine replied. He added that the Pentagon’s job was to develop military options, and understand the risks associated with them. “My main job is to always ensure that leaders understand those options and the risks,” Caine added.

title: Iran’s foreign minister describes moment of attack that killed Khamenei
author: Patrick Wintour
text:
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, has described how he was pulled from the rubble of a leadership compound after the US-Israeli airstrike that killed the country’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, on the first day of the war, and has survived since by constantly moving around the capital, Tehran, by car.
In an interview with the Iranian journalist Javad Mogouyi, Araghchi confirmed Israel and the US had accurate intelligence on the location of Khamenei and other officials, enabling them to target Iran’s senior leadership.
He said he had yet to meet the country’s new leader, Khamenei’s son Mojtaba, but said his appointment sent “a very important message to the world that there would be no change in the regime’s policies and ideals”.
Speaking to Mogouyi before the resumption of all-out hostilities 10 days ago, Araghchi said he had always doubted that negotiations with the US earlier this year would work, but said they had been necessary, even if there was only a 10% chance of success – not least to ensure there was no room for doubt that Iran had pursued diplomacy. “No one would be able to tell us that it was our fault,” he said.
In the interview published online on Sunday, Araghchi confirmed that Iran had offered the US a deal on its nuclear programme in the final round of talks in Geneva, but said Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, told him the following day that the mood in Washington had suddenly become more bellicose.
The joint US-Israeli strikes began shortly after 9am the next day, when senior officials had gathered for meetings at the ministry of intelligence, the strategic council on foreign policy, and the defence council.
“What matters, in my view, is the fact that Israel had intelligence about these meetings,” Araghchi said, adding: “This may point to a security gap that probably still exists. This needs to be fixed.”
Araghchi was reporting back to Khamenei’s deputy chief of staff, Ali Asghar Hijazi, when the building was shaken by three blasts within seconds – each closer than the last, he said. “The third explosion was almost next to our building. The section where Mr Hijazi’s office was located was directly hit, and the left side of the building was completely destroyed.”
Hijazi’s secretary was killed instantly, but Araghchi and Hijazi escaped the full force of the detonation.
“We were on the other side of the building, and after the explosion, the ceiling, walls, and everything collapsed on us. I grabbed Mr Hijazi’s hand, and we made our way through the beams and boards and pieces of wood, hearing the cries for help. Water was pouring from the ceiling. Everything was wrecked. We eventually got out, and I saw that various parts of the compound had been targeted.”
Araghchi was rushed to the foreign ministry by a passerby since his official car had been hit.
“For three days we were cut off from everything trying to find out who was alive and who had been martyred,” he said. “The enemy thought they could paralyse us by targeting leadership, but they failed.”
Araghchi said Iran had been prepared for such an attack, and had already drawn up plans to close the strategic strait of Hormuz if the supreme leader was targeted. The codename for such a scenario was “Code 110”, a reference to the clause of Iran’s constitution that lays out the supreme leader’s powers.
Araghchi said the US had decided to attack because it believed Iran’s government had been weakened abroad by blows to its proxies in Syria and Lebanon, and at home by economic protests – the speed and scale of which he admitted had surprised him.
Araghchi said regional governments had counselled Donald Trump against war, saying that attacking Iran would not be as easy as the US raid on Venezuela to abduct the then president, Nicolás Maduro. “Iran is different. Its support is a several-thousand-year civilisation, combined with Shia thought and beliefs about martyrdom. When these combine, they create something that cannot be easily defeated,” he said.
He told Mogouyi that Iran had warned neighbouring governments that any attack would be met with retaliation against targets in the region. “If Israel hits our nuclear facilities, we will hit theirs. Our missiles do not reach America, so we will hit their bases, which are unfortunately in your countries. If they hit our oil facilities, we will ensure that nobody in the region can sell oil,” he said.
He also said warnings to the Turkish government had prompted Ankara to shut down Trump’s plan to encourage a Kurdish revolt from Iraq into Iran. Turkey’s foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, “talked to the Americans and adopted a very firm position in this regard. A series of efforts foiled this plot,” Araghchi said.
He added that Iran was working to exacerbate divisions between the US and Israel. “There are sometimes conflicts of objectives and positions which can be played with,” he said, without giving details.
Araghchi said that after Israel’s 12-day bombing campaign against his country in 2025, Iran had improved its missile capabilities, reducing the time needed to reactivate a base after an attack from 10–15 hours to 35–40 minutes.
Discussing the choice of diplomacy or war, Araghchi said: “We do not fight unless the cost of not fighting is higher than the cost of fighting.”

title: Trump ally wins Republican primary for Arizona governor, setting up race against Katie Hobbs
author: Lauren Gambino
text:
Arizona voters on Tuesday chose their nominees for governor, Congress and other top offices, setting up a fall campaign that will test whether Republicans can reverse some of the Trump-era losses they suffered in a premier battleground state.
Andy Biggs, the hard-right congressman endorsed by Donald Trump, easily won the Republican nomination to challenge the incumbent Democrat, governor Katie Hobbs.
The race is expected to be among the most fiercely contested in the country, with control of the governor’s office carrying outsized national significance in a state that became “ground zero” for election denialism after Trump’s narrow loss there in 2020.
Biggs, a former chair of the House freedom caucus who was a central figure in the effort to overturn Trump’s election defeat, trounced fellow congressman David Schweikert, by appealing to the party’s deeply conservative base.
Throughout the campaign, Biggs and Schweikert offered constrasting visions for reclaiming the governorship. Schweikert, who gave up his toss-up congressional seat to run for governor after eight terms, argued that Biggs’ hard-right politics and unswerving embrace of the president had allowed Democrats to make gains in once-ruby-red Arizona.
But Republican voters in Arizona, as they have across the country, followed the president’s lead, even though Trump’s candidates have repeatedly fallen short in the state’s most competitive general election contests.
Businessmen Ken Miceli and Scott Neely were also vying for the nomination. Hobbs, who flipped the seat from red to blue in 2022, ran unopposed.
Arizona has transformed in recent years from a Republican stronghold into a competitive swing state, fueled by rapid population growth, shifting suburban voting patterns around Phoenix and an influx of college-educated voters.
In the decade since Trump’s election in 2016, Democrats have gained control of the top three statewide offices – governor, attorney general and secretary of state – as well as both US Senate seats. Trump narrowly carried Arizona in 2024 after losing the state four years earlier – a defeat he unsuccessfully sought to overturn.
This year, Republicans are contending with unfavorable national political conditions. Historically, the president’s party loses ground in the midterm elections, and Democrats are hopeful they can seize control of the House – and possibly the Senate, riding a wave of discontent over high gas prices and an unpopular Iran war that have dragged down Trump’s approval ratings. Two toss-up House districts in Arizona are key to that effort.
Arizona’s first congressional district, anchored in affluent Scottsdale, has long been a Democratic target as the suburbs shifted away from the Republican party over the past decade.
Two years ago, Schweikert won re-election with just under 52% of the vote, narrowly defeating Amish Shah, a former state lawmaker who Democrats appeared poised to re-nominate on Tuesday.
His challenger, the former local news anchor Marlene Galán-Woods, also sought the nomination two years ago. This year, Galán-Woods, the widow of former Republican attorney general Grant Woods, who publicly broke with his party over Trump, earned the controversial backing of the Democratic congressional campaign committee.
Shah will face Republican Jay Feely, a former Arizona Cardinals kicker, in November. Feely faced Joseph Chaplik, a former state lawmaker, and John Trobough, a technology and telecommunications executive, in his party’s primary.
In the sixth congressional district, which extends from the suburbs of Tucson to the US-Mexico border, encompassing much of south-eastern Arizona, Democrats hope national headwinds facing the president’s party will dislodge Republican congressman Juan Ciscomani, who is seeking a third term. Democrat JoAnna Mendoza, a Marine Corps veteran, was running unopposed.
Meanwhile, the contest to succeed Biggs in the safely Republican fifth congressional district has drawn unusual attention. The Trump-backed Republican nominee, former Pinal County Sheriff Mark Lamb, spent the closing weeks of the primary campaign confronting allegations of sexual misconduct and abuse of power reported in a multi-part investigation by the Arizona Republic. Prosecutors found no basis for criminal charges, and Trump has re-affirmed his support for Lamb, who has denied wrongdoing.
He will face Democrat Elizabeth Lee, a nurse, in the general election.
Elsewhere, Republicans chose their nominees for two top state positions that Democrats see as critical to pushing back against the Trump administration.
Warren Petersen, president of the Arizona senate, was leading the Republican primary race to take on Democrat Kris Mayes for attorney general. Mayes, an outspoken critic of Trump, won the office in 2022 by just 280 votes after an automatic recount, making it one of the closest statewide races in Arizona history. He was competing for the nomination against Rodney Glassman, a former Democrat who was the party’s Senate nominee against John McCain in 2010 before joining the Republican party.
Alex Kolodin, a Republican state representative and attorney who helped lead failed legal efforts to overturn Arizona’s 2020 and 2022 election results, will face Democratic secretary of state Adrian Fontes, in November for the office that will oversee elections in a swing state during the 2028 presidential race. Fontes has cast himself as a bulwark against Trump’s election denialism while overseeing elections in one of the nation’s most closely watched battleground states.
Kolodin defeated Gina Swoboda, a former state party chair who abandoned an earlier bid for Schweikert’s House seat to instead run for secretary of state.
Tuesday’s primary also settled tight contests in legislative races across Arizona, where Republicans hold slim majorities in both chambers of the state capitol.

title: Saudis and US strike deal for kingdom to enrich uranium, reports say
author: Agencies; Guardian staff reporter
text:
Donald Trump has approved an agreement with Saudi Arabia that could provide the kingdom with uranium enrichment capability for its civilian nuclear programme, according to news reports citing people familiar with the matter.
The people, who were not authorised to comment publicly about the yet to be formally announced decision, said the agreement may be announced as early as Wednesday. The deal was reported by both the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times.
The deal is expected to last 30 years and is also expected to involve US firms in developing the programme. It could allow for the building of a uranium enrichment facility in Saudi Arabia after a joint US-Saudi study.
It is expected to be submitted to Congress for review where it could face headwinds among lawmakers who fear that helping the Saudis fulfil their longstanding desire to enrich their own uranium would open new rounds of nuclear proliferation and competition.
Saudi Arabia is a member state of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), a Vienna-based agency that promotes peaceful nuclear work but also does inspections to make sure countries do not have clandestine atomic weapons programmes.
The agreement is not expected to include the IAEA’s “additional protocol”, which would allow for more monitoring, inspections and verification, according to one of the people who revealed it.
The expected announcement comes amid the war against Iran launched by the US and Israel – in part on the premise of wiping out Tehran’s ability to develop a nuclear weapon. Iran insists its nuclear enrichment programme is peaceful, but has previously boasted of enriching uranium to the brink of what is needed to explode a nuclear bomb.
The White House and Saudi officials in Riyadh did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the decision, which was first reported by the Journal.
Both Trump and former president Joe Biden tried to reach a nuclear deal with the kingdom to share American technology.
But non-proliferation experts warn any centrifuges – used to enrich uranium – within Saudi Arabia could open the door to a weapons programme for the kingdom, something its de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, has not ruled out if Iran obtains an atomic bomb.
Enrichment is not an automatic path to a nuclear weapon – there are other steps, such as mastering the use of synchronised conventional high explosives. It does however open the door to weaponisation, which has fuelled the concerns of the west over Iran’s programme.
Trump’s energy secretary, Chris Wright, travelled to Saudi Arabia in 2025 shortly before Trump visited the kingdom and discussed building out the kingdom’s commercial nuclear power industry with his Saudi counterpart. The US department of energy did not immediately respond to requests for comment late on Tuesday.
Saudi Arabia and nuclear-armed Pakistan signed a mutual defence pact after Israel launched an attack on Qatar targeting Hamas officials. Pakistan’s defence minister then said his nation’s nuclear programme “will be made available” to Saudi Arabia if needed, something seen as a warning for Israel, long believed to be the Middle East’s only nuclear-armed state.
The United Arab Emirates, a neighbour to Saudi Arabia, signed what is referred to as a “123 agreement” with the US to build its Barakah nuclear power plant with South Korean assistance. But the UAE did so without seeking enrichment, something non-proliferation experts have held up as the “gold standard” for countries wanting nuclear power.
Associated Press

title: Wednesday briefing: How Trump’s Iran gamble has produced a crisis reshaping the global order
author: Hettie O'Brien
text:
Good morning. Within two hours of entering No 10 on Monday afternoon, Andy Burnham had his first call with Donald Trump. After chit-chatting about the football (both agreed England had an “excellent tournament”) and Manchester (our new prime minister invited the president to visit the city Trump once described as a “town”), they got on to far trickier territory: the strait of Hormuz.
The US has attacked Iran for the eleventh consecutive night, hitting aircraft hangars and drone storage sites across the country. It came after Iran launched retaliatory strikes on US air bases and neighbouring Gulf states, which have accused it of deliberately targeting desalination plants that are essential to life in the region. Each side now claims it is preventing the other from gaining control over the strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of the world’s oil was shipped before the war began. Vessels carrying crucial shipments of oil, gas and fertiliser remain at a standstill.
“Operation Epic Fury” started with the aim of regime change. Since then, its objective has morphed into reopening the strait and undoing the damage caused by the US and Israel’s decision to start the war. The president drastically underestimated Iran’s capacity for enduring pain, and is now trying to bomb his way out of a conflict that he created. For today’s First Edition, I spoke to Vali Nasr, professor of International Affairs and Middle East Studies and author of Iran’s Grand Strategy, about the war over the world’s most critical bottleneck. That’s after the headlines.
Five big stories
- 
  UK politics | Andy Burnham is under mounting pressure to explain how he will pay for his policy pledges as he implored his new cabinet to examine “all possible ways” to tackle the cost of living crisis. 
- 
  UK news | A man has appeared in court charged with the murder of the former MP and Reform UK spokesperson Ann Widdecombe. Joshua Kerry, 28, is accused of killing the former Conservative minister at her home in Haytor, Devon, by hitting her on the head with a hammer 21 times. 
- 
  Middle East | The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, told the Senate the US-Israel war on Iran had cost $37.5bn so far, as he faced lawmakers furious over the conflict’s soaring price tag and the deaths last week of three American service members. 
- 
  Climate crisis | About 23 million people will be banned from using hosepipes by this weekend, as England and Wales moves closer to drought status. 
- 
  Ukraine | Volodymyr Zelenskyy has fired Ukraine’s commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi and offered a “prominent position” to the defence minister he sacked last week in a move that sparked nationwide protests. 
In depth: ‘In his mind, this was a legacy-building transformation’
“I’m not going to start wars,” Donald Trump told voters on election night in 2024. His decision to bomb Iran on 28 February in partnership with Benjamin Netanyahu was astonishing both in its aggression and its audacious break with this promise. Trump did nothing to prepare the US for war, gave seemingly no thought to the fact that Iran would inevitably hold the strait hostage if it came under attack, and resorted to contradictory explanations for his decision. In the war’s early days, he described “what we did in Venezuela” as a model for what he hoped to achieve. “He thought he would go down in history as the American president who had resolved the Iran problem,” Nasr told me. “In his mind, this was a legacy-building transformation that would be quick and cost-free.”
That has proven a fatal miscalculation. Pete Hegseth, the US self-styled “secretary of war”, said the early US strikes that killed Iran’s Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei, had “cut off the head of the snake.” But regime change is now a distant prospect. Trump underestimated the resilience of the Iranian regime and overestimated the power of protests against it. After just five months, his misadventure is as unpopular with American voters as the Vietnam war was six years in. It could yet escalate into a wider regional conflict, with the Houthis threatening a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia. Even Trump – whose private firm, The Trump Organization, is at work on a skyscraper in Dubai – won’t be insulated from the consequences of this violence.
What happened to the ceasefire?
The memorandum of understanding, a vague, short document that the US and Iran signed on 17 June, gave a brief respite from the strikes and (supposedly) initiated a 60-day negotiation period in which time both sides could reach permanent agreement on – among other things – the future of the strait. But it broke down when Iran fired on three commercial tankers that had used a shipping lane close to the shores of Oman, rather than a route off the Iranian coast approved by Tehran. “When ceasefires are violated, you have two options; either react to preserve the ceasefire, or use the violation as an excuse to end it,” Nasr says.
Trump went with the latter option, calling Iran’s leaders “scum” and declaring the ceasefire “over” earlier this month. This week, the US energy secretary Chris Wright said the US mission had shifted towards ensuring oil shipments could move through the strait. It’s worth remembering that the strait had never been closed for an extended period. Before 28 February, ships had been sailing through it without obstruction. The US is now framing the potential of a return to this old status quo as a victory.
Iran and the US are still negotiating, and Tehran has signalled its desire to permanently control the strait, including by charging tolls on passing vessels. “The US is now in a situation where it either has a long, protracted war, which would keep the strait closed, or keeps escalating to the next level with the hope of knocking Iran out,” Nasr says.
A serious misjudgment
There are signs that Trump and Netanyahu seriously misjudged the likelihood that Iran would seize control of the strait. In an interview earlier this year, Netanyahu admitted “the problem of the Hormuz strait became understood as the war went on.” As our diplomatic editor Patrick Wintour wrote at the time, in a piece suggesting the consequences of Trump’s excursion could prove greater than the Vietnam war, this was an “astonishing admission.” The closure of the strait is the type of doomsday scenario that previous administrations, and most Iran experts, would have considered.
But the US government now has very few Iran experts, because Trump has instead chosen to surround himself with a royal court of loyalists. Nate Swanson, a former state department representative on Trump’s Iran negotiating team, was forced out earlier this year after far-right activist Laura Loomer accused him of disloyalty.
“Folks who’ve watched this Iranian system … would have told [Trump]: ‘They’re not businessmen from New York. They’re made of a different type of DNA’,” Alex Vatanka, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute in Washington DC, recently told Guardian US political correspondent, Robert Tait.
Consequences, consequences
Inflation caused by rising oil prices is making everyday life more expensive and hiking the costs of borrowing for governments (including Burnham’s here in the UK). If there is no agreement until 2027, some are predicting global growth could fall by 1.3%, if not more. Europe may be uniquely exposed: since the Russia-Ukraine war, the continent has turned towards the Middle East for its gas, particularly to Qatar, which has had to slow production during the conflict. We could be facing a winter of shortages, bringing to mind the 1970s oil crisis, when the British government enforced power cuts to conserve energy supplies.
Who’s in charge of the sea?
Many of Trump’s proposed solutions to the conflict seem to have been thought up on the spot. He briefly suggested that the US could charge tolls on ships entering the strait in exchange for safe passage, despite European leaders and even Marco Rubio, his own secretary of state, having previously said these would be incompatible with international law. The fact the US and Iran have even proposed such tolls is a sign of the wilful disregard for international law that has become a defining feature of this conflict (notably, Iran, the US and Israel are among a small handful of nations that don’t ratify the UN convention on the laws of the sea). Freedom of navigation is a cornerstone of international law: without it, shipping starts to resemble a protection racket, where nations extract fees from passing vessels.
Some experts now worry that other shipping routes could become more militarised, as coastal nations watching Iran use the strait as the ultimate bargaining chip try to take advantage of other important waterways. “A lot of other countries that feel they’re like Iran, and could use passageways as a deterrent” Nasr says. “If nations like the US and Israel can attack your country at any time, you’re going to resort to whatever you can in order to protect yourself.”
What else we’ve been enjoying
-

- 
  Ed Miliband was trying to start a green energy revolution in Britain. Now he’s at the Foreign Office, what happens to that agenda? I enjoyed reading this piece by Fiona Harvey, which has some answers. Hettie 
- 
  “It’s a crime that alters your whole reality.” Anna Moore on the impact of crime, here on the survivor-led campaign to end drug-facilitated sexual rape. Libby 
- 
  If (like me) you feel creeped out by reading about Meta’s new “smartglasses”, which allow wearers to film people without their consent, it’s worth reading this piece by Gaby Hinsliff. Hettie 
- 
  Herald writer Neil Mackay makes a powerful argument that the future health of the Scottish independence movement depends on Burnham’s success or failure in Westminster. Libby 
Sport
Cycling | Remco Evenepoel took back-to-back stage wins in the Tour de France, and eroded some of Tadej Pogacar’s overall lead, with victory in the stage 16 time trial from Evian to Thonon-les-Bains.
Tennis | The French Open has become the first grand slam tournament to offer players a share of the event’s revenue in a significant step forward in the row over prize money.
Football | La Liga’s president, Javier Tebas, has accused Fifa of “destroying the football industry” and called for its president, Gianni Infantino, to quit.
The front pages
“Burnham implores cabinet to find ways to tackle cost of living crisis”, is the Guardian’s front page today, the Times writes “Burnham signals cuts to pay for spending pledges”, and the i Paper’s take is “Cost of living, cost of living, cost of living”. The Mail asks “Who’s going to pay the bill for Andy’s largesse?” and the FT has “Burnham backs away from rise in tax allowance ‘to show fiscal discipline’”.
Elsewhere, the Telegraph leads on “Pc Harper’s killers set for early release”. The Mirror, Sun, Metro and Express all splash on details from court with variations of “Ann ‘hit 21 times with hammer’”.
The Latest
US soldiers killed: has Trump lost control of Iran war?
The US has carried out a fresh round of strikes against Iran, after three US soldiers were killed in action. The Pentagon has also admitted that nearly 100 US service members have been injured over the last two weeks, as Tehran launched a wave of reprisals to the tenth consecutive nights of attacks, even as peace talks mediated by Pakistan continue. A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad
Yotam Maron, a key organiser in the Occupy Wall Street movement which spawned a global network in 2011, has worked on multiple social movements since then. He identifies a “politics of powerlessness” which too often hobbles them, mistaking “a healthy distrust of institutional power for a failure to build a strong, coherent strategy for political change”. Since then, he founded the Wildfire Project, a training organisation for grassroots groups to counter that misplaced internal logic and argues now, even with Democrat socialists in the ascendancy across some parts of the US, that people power must continue to be built through movements not elected politicians.

title: Mamdani urges US government to arrest Netanyahu if Israeli PM visits US
author: Robert Mackey
text:
Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, acknowledged on Tuesday he does not have the authority to arrest Benjamin Netanyahu, but urged US federal authorities to do so if the Israeli prime minister visits the US later this year.
“Benjamin Netanyahu is a war criminal, the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people,” Mamdani said in a video posted to social media.
Mamdani said he believed the international criminal court warrant for Netanyahu’s arrest over alleged war crimes was justified, but admitted he lacked the legal authority to enforce it.
“My administration has reviewed every avenue available under applicable law to determine whether New York City could execute the international criminal court’s arrest warrant if Benjamin Netanyahu came here,” Mamdani said. “It is clear that we do not have the independent legal authority to enforce this warrant.
“The federal government, however, does – and I call on them to join the ICC and execute this warrant,” the mayor added. “And I want to be equally clear: Benjamin Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City, nor is any other war criminal at large.”
Netanyahu is expected to travel to New York in September for the UN general assembly.
Mamdani said last week he was reviewing whether he would be able to arrest Netanyahu during that visit, after pledging to do so during his mayoral campaign last year.
“I believe that prime minister Netanyahu belongs in The Hague,” Mamdani said in reference to the Dutch city where the international criminal court, which issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in 2024, is located.
The US does not recognize the ICC’s authority and is not a party to it.
His remarks drew rebuke from Donald Trump, who insisted Netanyahu “will not be arrested” on US soil.
Trump said in a social media post Netanyahu is “fighting against the Islamic Republic of Iran” and “the only ones that should be arrested are the people that led Iran into this unprecedented spiral of death and destruction”.
Netanyahu, meanwhile, said he was “not concerned” about Mamdani’s comments.
